detail.abstract: This study presents the design and analytical evaluation of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) frameworks tailored specifically for FinTech ecosystems. The proposed approach integrates automated risk assessment, continuous compliance monitoring, and explainable governance mechanisms to address the growing complexity, velocity, and regulatory sensitivity of digital financial services. Building on prior work in AI-enabled governance and compliance automation (Olawore et al.; Putchakayala and Yallavula), the study adopts a qualitative and comparative research methodology. Existing AI-based GRC and governance models are systematically synthesised, abstracted into a unified conceptual framework, and evaluated through qualitative performance mapping across three critical dimensions: security effectiveness, compliance agility, and auditability (Hlatshwayo). The analysis reveals that AI-driven GRC frameworks significantly enhance fraud detection accuracy through adaptive learning and behavioural pattern recognition, while enabling faster regulatory responsiveness via real-time compliance analytics. In addition, these frameworks improve cross-platform risk visibility by consolidating heterogeneous data streams into unified governance dashboards, thereby reducing reliance on manual oversight processes and lowering operational governance overhead. Evidence from AI-powered payment fraud signature generation further demonstrates the practical benefits of automated, intelligence-driven risk controls in high-volume FinTech environments. The study concludes that AI-driven GRC frameworks represent a foundational shift in how modern FinTech ecosystems can be secured and governed. However, to ensure long-term effectiveness and stakeholder trust, such frameworks must embed robust explainability, transparency, and ethical auditing mechanisms as core design principles (Odedina).

title: (Mis)measurement of Income Shifting
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business, WU Vienna University of Economics and Business and Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: (Mis)measurement of Income Shifting

publicationDetails.detailsText: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series No. 2026-01
publicationDetails.journalName: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the reliability of financial statement data for measuring cross-border income shifting. Using a novel dataset of Austrian corporate tax returns matched with financial statement data, we estimate a tax semi-elasticity of taxable income reported on tax returns of-0.9. When we use financial statement profits instead of taxable income, the semi-elasticity decreases by more than 50%. This result suggests that financial statement profits understate the extent of income shifting observed in tax return data. As a result, studies that rely on financial statement data are likely to underestimate income shifting at the firm level. We offer practical guidance on how to correct for biases arising from the disparity between financial statement profits and taxable income.

title: Beyond Explainability: Architectural Accountability in Public Sector Algorithms
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Beyond Explainability: Architectural Accountability in Public Sector Algorithms
detail.abstract: Digital rights frameworks assume that transparency enables accountability. This Commentary argues that algorithmic decision-making systems can satisfy formal transparency requirements while systematically undermining the accountability these rights are meant to protect. It identifies three mechanisms through which this occurs: bias amplification, where algorithms compound rather than average out biased inputs; governance filtering, where institutional reporting structures systematically remove uncomfortable truths before they reach training data; and accountability displacement, where automation breaks the chain of human responsibility. Drawing on two evidence streams — Freedom of Information research across 175 NHS trusts documenting contemporary governance structures, and National Audit Office investigations documenting the 2017 WannaCry attack — this Commentary empirically demonstrates the governance filtering mechanism: structures existed, yet structures failed, because reporting hierarchies systematically diluted the urgency of warnings before they reached decision-makers. Any algorithmic system trained on such institutionally filtered data would inherit, not correct, these blind spots. The Commentary proposes "architectural accountability" as a policy response: explicit allocation of decision rights, escalation triggers, assumption registers, and upstream data audits. Protecting digital rights in algorithmic governance requires designing for accountability, not merely accuracy.

title: The Osmotic Model of Communication: A Process-Oriented Framework for Understanding Contemporary Censorship

detail.title: The Osmotic Model of Communication: A Process-Oriented Framework for Understanding Contemporary Censorship

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Osmotic Model of Communication as a process-oriented framework for analysing contemporary forms of censorship in complex media environments. Rather than treating censorship as overt prohibition, the model conceptualises communication as a flow driven by informational asymmetries and regulated through selective permeability within media systems. It argues that censorship operates by modulating the conditions of circulation rather than by fully blocking information. The model identifies three interrelated dimensions of censorship: speed (temporal control), reach (selective restriction of audience access), and framing (discursive shaping of meaning). These mechanisms can converge into coherent systems of information control without constant central coordination or explicit bans. Illustrated through anonymized observations from the Hungarian media environment, the framework is developed as a general analytical tool applicable across media regimes and platform-based communication, opening avenues for comparative and empirical research on subtle forms of censorship.

title: Local Competition Promotes Hurtful Behaviour Towards Unknown Others
affiliations: Purdue University - Krannert School of Management, Maastricht University, University of Amsterdam - Faculty of Economics and Business (FEB) and University of Amsterdam - Faculty of Economics and Business (FEB)

detail.title: Local Competition Promotes Hurtful Behaviour Towards Unknown Others
detail.abstract: Humans frequently cooperate to achieve benefits unattainable through selfish behaviour. Punishment of free-riders is key for sustaining cooperation but also costly, raising questions about the origins of such behaviour. Some evolutionary models suggest that individuals may be willing to hurt unknown others in competitive environments. However, empirical evidence about the effect of the scale of competition on strategies involving hurtful behaviour in human groups, such as spite, retaliation for hurting, and punishment of free-riders, is missing. Using a laboratory experiment, we manipulate the scale of competition to investigate its influence on hurtful and helpful behaviours, between unknown humans in an indirect reciprocity game. We observe distinct behavioural patterns between local and global competition. When competition is local and thus confined to take place within isolated groups we find frequent hurting as an expression of spite and retaliation. In contrast, when competition extends globally across several groups, hurting is used primarily for punishment of free-riders whereas helping behaviour is rewarded, which together promotes cooperation. Thus, while isolated competition fosters inefficient, antisocial behaviour, global competition encourages prosociality and cooperation.

detail.title: ESG Rating Disagreement and ESG Disclosure: A Literature Review
detail.abstract: We examine the insights from prior studies on the question of whether management-provided Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosure can reduce ESG-related rating disagreement (hereafter, ESG disagreement). Specifically, we summarize evidence from prior studies on: (1) what ESG disagreement is, (2) the importance of ESG disagreement, (3) the causes of ESG disagreement, (4) potential solutions for mitigating ESG disagreement, and (5) the specific role of ESG disclosure as a potential solution. We outline directions and provide insights for future research in this area.

title: The EU's Evolving Approach to Cross-Border Data Flows: From 'Non-Negotiable' to 'Manageable'
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Institute for Information Law (IViR)

detail.title: The EU's Evolving Approach to Cross-Border Data Flows: From 'Non-Negotiable' to 'Manageable'

keywords: Cross-border data flows EU digital trade agreements; GDPR international data transfers; Data protection exception (conditions of general application); CPTPP model and interoperability

detail.abstract: Over the past decade, cross-border data flows have become a flashpoint in international trade policy, forcing governments to reconcile the economic value of digital trade with domestic objectives such as privacy, security, and digital sovereignty. This chapter traces the European Union’s (EU) evolving approach, arguing that it has shifted from treating privacy and data protection as “non-negotiable” constraints on trade negotiations to a more “manageable” framework that preserves core protections while accepting trade-oriented disciplines on data flows. It first maps the EU’s trajectory from early resistance to binding data-flow commitments (including the 2018 “horizontal provisions”) to the EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement and, more recently, the EU’s digital trade instruments with Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, which broaden prohibitions on restrictions and recalibrate the data-protection exception toward an ex ante design requirement (transfer mechanisms must be available under “conditions of general application”). It then tests this emerging template against the EU’s internal personal data transfer framework under the GDPR as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the EU and the European Data Protection Board, identifying tensions where the EU framework may fail to “enable” transfers for significant categories of transactions (notably where relevant contractual tools are missing or where guidance effectively forecloses transfers absent workable supplementary measures). Finally, it situates the EU’s new template relative to the CPTPP model, showing partial convergence alongside enduring structural differences. The chapter concludes with policy options to reduce internal/external inconsistency, including adoption of missing transfer instruments, more granular guidance on “essential equivalence,” and longer-term international solutions to government-access risks.

title: Brazil's Bill No. 4675/2025: Regulating Systemically Relevant Economic Actors
affiliations: University of Sussex - School of Law, Politics and Sociology

detail.title: Brazil's Bill No. 4675/2025: Regulating Systemically Relevant Economic Actors
detail.abstract: In 2025, Brazil proposed Bill No. 4675/2025 to address competition concerns in digital markets. The proposal followed a period of enforcement activity involving large platforms, a failed earlier legislative initiative, and a public consultation led by the Ministry of Finance. This chapter explains how the Brazilian bill is structured and what problems it seeks to address. It examines three core elements of the proposal: the designation of systemically relevant economic agents, the use of ecosystem characteristics to identify competition risks, and the possibility of imposing tailored obligations and monitoring their implementation through the competition authority. The chapter situates these choices within Brazil's constitutional and institutional approach to competition law and contrasts them with regulatory models adopted in other jurisdictions, including the EU, UK, Germany and Japan. In doing so, it shows how the Brazilian proposal gives rise to a hybrid regulatory arrangement that combines preventive tools with competition-law procedures to address the structural features of digital markets.

title: Stability and inclusion in a Delayed Wage-Competition Model in a Resilient Economy
affiliations: Ryerson University and Universidad de Oriente

detail.title: Stability and inclusion in a Delayed Wage-Competition Model in a Resilient Economy

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not apply
declarations.funderStatement: No funded

detail.abstract:
This paper addresses the traditional problem of the relationship between labor and capital, which uses Goodwin's predator-prey metaphor. However, we reformulate it by assuming that the struggle arises from the competition for wage distribution between two classes of labor competing for the same finite source of employment: the highly skilled and the low-skilled. These groups are involved in a dynamic with a time lag resulting from several factors, including the time spent on job applications, resumes in inboxes, and other aspects related to employee selection.

As the economy does not forget all at once, but rather carries echoes of what was, our model is based on a distributed time lag. The system with a time lag translates into a framework of 5-dimensional ordinary differential equations. We discover endogenous economic cycles, expressed by oscillations that emerge from a Hopf bifurcation. The procedures in this work are not merely diagnostic; they propose a more humane and forward-looking policy repertoire anchored in pressing realities of 21st-century work, such as the silent advance of automation, the polarizing force of skills-based technological change, and the hopeful yet uncertain emergence of green jobs. These are not abstract disruptions; they reconfigure bargaining power, recalibrate demand, and ultimately determine who thrives and who is left behind. This is where theory becomes ethical.

Beyond the purely theoretical, we propose grounding the model in the experience of any real-world resilient economy. In our case, Canada presents a compelling example, not only because of its readily available data but also due to its own internal tension between a thriving digital sector and a vulnerable service structure. Using national and OECD labor data, we engage in the empirical dialogue that transforms equations into narratives and conditions of stability into policy perspectives. We calibrate the model with respect to Canada (2023); in this case, the baseline “Reactive Stasis” scenario exhibits systemic employment collapse when wage‑competition terms dominate logistic recovery. We develop two variants of policy-oriented approaches: a parity-constrained stabilization that sustains high employment and nearly equal wage shares, and an inclusive configuration that ensures non-negative growth in low-skill wage shares

title: How Many Financial Advisers do you Need?
affiliations: Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (AMSS), University of Warwick - Warwick Business School and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Center for Forecasting Science; Academy of Mathematics and Systems Sciences

detail.title: How Many Financial Advisers do you Need?
detail.abstract: We study how investors aggregate recommendations of multiple financial advisers under uncertainty and behavioral constraints. Investors lack knowledge of market parameters and, therefore, rely on financial advisers who observe heterogeneous private signals and recommend investment strategies that maximize client utility. We model the investor's aggregation problem within a rational expectations equilibrium, subject to bounded rationality constraints capturing limited financial literacy, conformism, and regret aversion under ambiguity. These constraints restrict admissible aggregation policies to nonnegative weighted averages of advisers' recommendations and preclude direct use of price information. Within this framework, we characterize the investor's optimal aggregation policy and study the optimal number of advisers to consult with. We find that there is an equivalent signal precision that provides a sufficient statistic for evaluating aggregation policies, thereby reducing the original problem to a deterministic problem maximizing the equivalent signal precision. The optimal aggregation policy exhibits two key properties: it assigns strictly positive weight to at least two advisers, and it endogenously disregard advisers whose information quality is sufficiently low. Consequently, consulting a small number of high-quality advisers dominates both reliance on a single expert and indiscriminate aggregation of many sources.

title: Electoral Inequalities and Outcomes in France: An Algorithmic Redistricting Approach

detail.title: Electoral Inequalities and Outcomes in France: An Algorithmic Redistricting Approach
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of electoral geography and redistricting on political representation in France. Using an algorithmic approach, we generate 1,000 alternative redistricting plans for 72 departments based on the 2017 legislative election. These simulated plans allow us to analyze two main issues. First, we study how alternative district maps affect electoral outcomes. We show that the electoral performance of the far right and the right is highly sensitive to redistricting, while the left exhibits intermediate sensitivity and the center limited sensitivity. We propose a definition to identify atypical redistricting plans at the departmental level associated with partisan bias, which can be linked to gerrymandering. Second, we assess how French electoral geography may generate inequalities in representation. Because voters in small constituencies carry more electoral weight than those in large ones, we analyze population imbalances across constituencies. Moreover, as political preferences are not proportionally distributed, some groups may be overrepresented or underrepresented. We examine how electoral geography may structurally misrepresent certain groups of voters. Beyond voting preferences, we conduct the same analysis for groups defined by socioeconomic characteristics.

title: The Illegality of Reciprocal Tariffs and Their Subsequent Agreements under International Trade Law
affiliations: University of Oxford - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Illegality of Reciprocal Tariffs and Their Subsequent Agreements under International Trade Law
detail.abstract: Earlier this year, the United States imposed reciprocal tariffs, after which a range of countries and regions-including the United Kingdom, Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Japan, the European Union, South Korea, Thailand, and Cambodia-entered into bilateral trade agreement frameworks with the United States. The extent to which these tariffs and subsequent frameworks contravene existing multilateral trade rules warrants close scrutiny. This study finds that concerns arise not only from the reciprocal tariffs themselves, but also from the numerous provisions in the subsequent agreements that appear to breach core principles such as most-favourednation treatment and the general prohibition on quantitative restrictions. These provisions risk coercing other countries into unlawful commitments, thereby destabilizing the multilateral trading system. It is therefore imperative to address reciprocal tariffs in order to safeguard the foundations of the multilateral order. Special caution is needed against the proliferation of a complex web of bilateral arrangements forged through negotiations following the imposition of reciprocal tariffs, as such developments may indirectly dismantle the multilateral trade system.

title: Causal Images and Aggregate Dynamics
affiliations: Virginia Tech

detail.title: Causal Images and Aggregate Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper studies what aggregate macro time series reveal about agents' subjective causal models. Agents hold heterogeneous ``causal images,'' directed graphs over output, inflation, and interest rates with coefficients and confidence weights. Although this heterogeneity is high dimensional, aggregation collapses it to six ``belief moments.'' Many distinct distributions of causal images sharing these moments generate identical aggregate dynamics, establishing exact observational equivalence. Perceived causal structure is fundamentally underidentified from standard macro data. Changes in belief moments can nonetheless alter whether equilibrium adjustment is monotone or oscillatory, and forecast-equivalent beliefs can persist when performance-based learning exerts weak selection pressure.

title: Algorithmic Harm: A Response to Critics
affiliations: Harvard Law School and New York University School of Law

detail.title: Algorithmic Harm: A Response to Critics
detail.abstract: In our 2025 book, Algorithmic Harm, we contend that the use of algorithms can benefit consumers in many ways (largely because of greater personalization), but that it can also cause harm in the face of information deficits and behavioral biases (again, largely because of greater personalization). Unsophisticated consumers, as we call them, are especially vulnerable to algorithmic harm. In this short response to a set of excellent comments on our book, we explore some of the benefits of personalization; some of the costs of forbidding it; some challenges, in terms of feasibility, to our preferred approaches; and the intriguing question whether and in what sense algorithms might be said to have an unconscious.

title: No Glory in Prevention? The Case of the Audit Association of German Private Banks

detail.title: No Glory in Prevention? The Case of the Audit Association of German Private Banks

detail.abstract: This paper examines how non-statutory audit institutions emerge, persist, and adapt in changing regulatory environments. Focusing on on the audit association of German private banks (titled ‘Prüfungsverband deutscher Banken e.V.’, short ‘Prüfungsfverband’), an independent supervisory body within the deposit insurance scheme, we investigate how it has maintained extensive audit rights despite lacking formal regulatory authority. Drawing on organizational and institutional theory and using causal process tracing, we analyse how the Prüfungsverband has upheld its social license to operate since its establishment in 1969 through pivotal events such as the introduction of statutory deposit insurance and major insurance cases. We show that the Prüfungsverband’s governance model is a credible system of self-regulation, serving as a template for later legislative reforms. Although the institution is unique, the mechanisms identified, particularly the role of membership and collective oversight, offer broader insights into when and how private organizations can assume regulatory or supervisory functions.

title: Competition, Procurement and Learning-by-Doing in the Space Launch Industry
affiliations: Department of Economics,  and

detail.title: Competition, Procurement and Learning-by-Doing in the Space Launch Industry
detail.abstract: We estimate a dynamic model of the U.S. space launch industry. The model allows past launches to improve rocket reliability and lower launch costs. It also allows the government to make forward-looking procurement choices. We use the model to analyze policy-relevant issues in the recent history of the industry: the 2006 United Launch Alliance "merger-to-monopoly" and the effects of efficiencies in the form of learning synergies; innovations, such as SpaceX's Falcon 9 and ULA's recent introduction of Vulcan Centaur; the costs and benefits of forward-looking procurements; and, the trade-offs between the advantages of centralized control and possible inefficiencies.

title: Fertility, Taxation, and Redistribution in Aging Democracies
affiliations: and Hosei University

detail.title: Fertility, Taxation, and Redistribution in Aging Democracies
detail.abstract: This paper studies the political economy of fertility, taxation, and redistribution in aging democracies. We develop an overlapping-generations model in which households live for two periods, choose fertility endogenously, and vote over labor income taxes, consumption taxes, and pay-as-you-go pensions. Children are costly during working life but become future taxpayers who finance redistribution; however, future generations do not participate in current political decisions. Endogenous fertility interacts with majority voting to generate a demographic-political feedback. Higher taxes and more generous pensions increase the effective cost of children and reduce fertility. Lower fertility raises the relative political weight of retirees, leading to further expansion of redistribution. We show that a stationary political equilibrium exists and is unique under standard conditions but is generically inefficient: fertility is inefficiently low and redistribution toward current retirees is inefficiently high. The inefficiency arises from a fiscal externality created by the political exclusion of future taxpayers, rather than from market failures or myopia. We then analyze a simple institutional reform that links pension benefits to realized fertility. By pricing future fiscal contributions into current political payoffs, fertility-linked pensions decentralize the constrained efficient allocation. A calibration to Japan illustrates the quantitative relevance of the mechanism in a rapidly aging democracy.

title: Designing for Power: Covariates, Indices, and Efficiency in Survey Experiments
affiliations: Rice University,  and Rice University

detail.title: Designing for Power: Covariates, Indices, and Efficiency in Survey Experiments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

Any opinions, findings and conclusions, or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the NSF.

detail.abstract: Survey experiments are widely used across the social sciences, yet many are underpowered. We examine two well-known, but unevenly applied, strategies for improving statistical efficiency: covariate adjustment and multi-item index outcomes. We formally evaluate when these practices increase power and revisit over four hundred recent social science survey experiments to empirically assess their prevalence and effectiveness. We show these techniques reduce distinct sources of variance and function as complements, not substitutes, for increasing power. However, the majority of survey experiments omit these practices or employ them ineffectively by adjusting for generic demographic covariates that yield minimal precision gains. Only a small minority of studies use specialized covariates or index outcomes. Fewer than five percent combine both practices. Drawing on simulations based on recent studies, we argue designs combining specialized covariates with a short index outcome offer a practical and robust way to increase the statistical power of survey experiments.

detail.abstract:
The COVID-19 pandemic has caused wide devastation and disruption. Over seven million people died, trillions of dollars evaporated, and virtually everybody has been affected in one way or another. As the pandemic turned into an endemic and with the continuous passage of time, the traumatic experience relating to COVID-19 has slowly faded away. So do the many reforms that have been proposed for the TRIPS Agreement and the larger international intellectual property regime. The lack of attention to improve the pandemic preparedness of this regime is particularly disturbing, considering that many medical and public health experts have already predicted that another global pandemic will happen in the next decade or two.

This chapter begins by discussing three challenges that will inevitably arise when countries seek to make ad hoc adjustments to standards in the TRIPS Agreement and other instruments in the international intellectual property regime upon the arrival of the next global pandemic. The chapter then offers a proposal for deferred intellectual property rights that could be built into these instruments pre-emptively before those challenges arise. While I take the position that this proposal will help improve the instruments' pandemic preparedness, one could also view the proposal as an illustration of the many possible ways to enhance such preparedness.

title: Quantifying Minsky Cycles

detail.title: Quantifying Minsky Cycles
detail.abstract: We develop a novel sentiment measure derived from survey data to empirically validate the Minsky-Kindleberger view on financial crises. Using survey data from multiple countries, we decompose beliefs into components explained by public information that are orthogonal to optimal machine beliefs, constructing a framework that isolates sentiment and its dispersion among individuals. We show that deviations from machine-optimized benchmarks arise from systematic misaggregation of public information. The sentiment measure is validated through its predictive relationships with financial markets and belief dynamics consistent with heterogeneous-beliefs asset pricing theory. We extend this sentiment measure historically for a panel of 78 countries using machine learning models trained on BERT embeddings of historical news articles (1903-2020). The backcasted sentiment shows that shocks in median sentiment predict credit booms in the non-tradable corporate sector, which prior research has linked to financial crises, providing the first historically large-scale empirical validation of the Minsky cycle. We further show that sentiment, which is a misaggregation of public information, is influenced by memory-related dynamics, as the time elapsed since major crises and the share of young-to-old people in the population strongly predict surges in optimism even when recent economic developments are controlled for.

title: The Delegated Alpha Overlay (DAO): An ETF-Anchored Framework for Disciplined Active Portfolio Construction

detail.title: The Delegated Alpha Overlay (DAO): An ETF-Anchored Framework for Disciplined Active Portfolio Construction

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental interventions. Ethics approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Delegated Alpha Overlay (DAO), a portfolio construction framework designed to reconcile the structural advantages of passive investing with selective, disciplined active decisionmaking. DAO anchors capital in broad-market exchange-traded funds (ETFs) to capture long-term market compounding while sourcing stock-level alpha exclusively from the largest and most persistent holdings within selected sector ETFs. By delegating security selection to institutional capital flows and constraining active decisions to capital allocation, trimming, and rotation, DAO aims to reduce behavioral error, limit universe sprawl, and improve decision quality over time. The framework emphasizes diversification and correlation control across multiple structural layers and treats alpha as contextual and temporary rather than permanent. DAO is positioned as a flexible, repeatable system rather than a prescriptive allocation model, suitable for a wide range of investor profiles.

title: Financial Literacy in Bangalore Gig Workers: An Empirical Analysis

detail.title: Financial Literacy in Bangalore Gig Workers: An Empirical Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.ethicsApproval: Informed consent was obtained from all participants involved in the study. Participation was voluntary, and all respondents were assured of anonymity. No personally identifiable information (PII) was stored or published.

detail.abstract: This study examines the level of financial literacy among gig workers in Bangalore. Gig workers often face vulnerabilities due to a lack of job security and benefits. Using the "Capability Approach" model (Sen, 1999) this study underpins financial literacy as an important skill for gig workers to reach their financial goals. Based on previous research on financial literacy in India, focus group discussions were used to administer a 5-question quiz to 40 security guards, who represented gig workers in this study. The quiz assessed financial literacy across three main areas: Numerical Ability, Financial Knowledge, and Financial Awareness. These areas together indicated the participants' overall financial literacy. The main goal of this study was to find demographic factors that best predicted financial literacy levels. Using Bayesian logistic regression, the findings suggest that migrant workers had much lower odds of being financially literate compared to locals and scored particularly low on financial awareness. Age also mattered, with participants aged 30 to 39 showing lower skills in numeracy and knowledge than those under 30. These findings emphasize the need for targeted financial education and policy actions that address the unique challenges faced by migrant gig workers.

title: The Democracy Manual To Antitrust. Time To Revisit The More Economic Approach

detail.title: The Democracy Manual To Antitrust. Time To Revisit The More Economic Approach
detail.abstract: This article presents the Democracy Manual to Antitrust. This is needed as broad, open-textured competition principles may lead to invalid and ineffective EU competition enforcement. A case in point is the use of a more economic approach based on average consumer surplus. Getting the balance between the individual consumer and the Commission wrong, today's more economic approach contravenes the EU Treaties. The Democracy Manual to Antitrust provides authoritative guidance as to how to do better. First, it identifies the pre-constitutional, basic norm that governs the transfer of decision-making power from the individual to the collective and, based thereupon, ensures the objective validity of positive law creation, including competition law enforcement policy. Then, it clarifies how the basic norm governs the manner in which the constitutional lawmaker has organized efficient resource allocation in the EU Treaties and thus the balance of decision-making power between the individual consumer and the Commission in antitrust. Last, it criticizes the use of average consumer surplus for failing the basic norm when specifying the principles of 'fair consumer share' and 'no elimination of competition' as laid down in Article 101(3) TFEU. As it turns out, Pareto efficiency is the way forward in antitrust. Neo Pareto efficiency does not fit the legal framework of Article 101 TFEU. Other than claimed, Pareto efficiency does not frustrate but promote effective competition policy-making.

title: Local Governmental Big Financing with Public Debts and Cross-Region Investments: Evidence from China
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of Banking and Finance and University of International Business and Economics

detail.title: Local Governmental Big Financing with Public Debts and Cross-Region Investments: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: The cross-regional segmentation of investment and production is among the primary impediments to resource allocation efficiency. Employing a unique bond project-level dataset of industrial-zone bonds issued by Chinese local governments, we show evidence that government-led debt raising in public bond markets, earmarked for local construction projects, effectively catalyzes cross-region investments. Further evidence suggests that local aggregate total factor productivity and industrial structure upgrading benefit from this investment reallocation and enhanced spatial market integration. Our evidence points to a potential positive role of local government prudent borrowing in bond markets in smoothening capital mobility and fostering investment liberalization.

detail.abstract: This report examines regional disparities in UK equity finance using data covering 60,543 deals totaling £145.3bn invested across 25,002 companies from 2011 to 2025 Q3. We document intensifying geographic concentration, with London capturing 47.2% of deals and 57.0% of invested value, while concentration indices rose 74% between 2011 and 2024. Econometric analysis using propensity score matching reveals persistent regional disadvantages beyond firm characteristics. Regional firms secure 8-18% smaller deal sizes than comparable London firms, with largest discounts in Yorkshire and the Humber (-17.8%) and the Midlands. We estimate the UK's 2024 equity gap at £8.1bn unadjusted, compressing to £0.75bn after incorporating behavioural frictions, with approximately 72% concentrated in growth-stage rather than seedstage finance. Regional proportional gaps remain elevated in thinner markets-East Midlands (22%), West Midlands (11%)-versus London (3%), demonstrating persistent place-based constraints. The findings indicate the binding constraint has shifted to scale-up capital and inform policy interventions targeting regional equity market development.

Redistribution, as expected, leads to lower inequality but it does not necessarily reduce growth. Especially in settings characterized by high initial inequality, a high tax rate can produce similar wealth levels as without taxation while reducing inequality. title: Quietly Ahead: The Diverging R&D Productivity of Public and Private Firms
affiliations: Owen Graduate School of Management at Vanderbilt University and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), Swedish House of Finance

detail.title: Quietly Ahead: The Diverging R&D Productivity of Public and Private Firms
detail.abstract: Using 80 years of patent-level data, we show that unlisted firms are "quietly ahead" of stock market–listed firms in the innovation race. While unlisted firms produced less valuable innovations for much of the twentieth century, they have risen to a leading position in innovation value this century. This reversal is not explained by changes in patent characteristics or by shifts in market multiples applied to those characteristics. Instead, it reflects differences in technology-field allocation: beginning in the 1980s, unlisted firms reallocated R&D toward fields with rising market valuations and away from declining ones. A simple conceptual lens highlights how nimble reallocation toward high-value fields becomes more valuable as technological opportunities grow more dispersed and persistent. Unlisted firms—especially young and first-time patenters—adjust more nimbly to emerging value signals, aided by venture capital. As a result, their share of aggregate R&D value-add has more than tripled since 1985, despite stable patent shares and faster R&D spending growth among listed firms.

title: Trademarks Without Confusion: Can Brand Rights Rescue Trademark Law?
affiliations: Stanford Law School and UCLA School of Law

detail.title: Trademarks Without Confusion: Can Brand Rights Rescue Trademark Law?
detail.abstract:
We have two very different trademark systems in this country. The traditional one protects consumers against being confused into buying a product by similar trademarks on similar goods. That system has been around for hundreds of years, is established in the statute, and is what courts and commentators think of when they talk about trademark law. A second, more recent set of cases effectively provides some trademark owners with a very different right – a right to prevent misappropriation of their brand identity. This second system, which we call brand rights, isn’t expressly separate from the traditional trademark law, but both its purposes and effects are radically different than that law. Because litigants and courts intermingle these cases, the rise of brand rights has led to dramatic and unwarranted expansions in trademark law more generally. And because courts still think of the laudable purposes of traditional trademark law when considering brand right cases, they don’t impose any of the limits they might otherwise require of a new property right that gives someone plenary control over a word or symbol.
            In the past, we, like other scholars, have resisted the expansion of trademark law. But brand rights, it seems, are here to stay. We don’t intend to revisit that debate here. Drawing on a series of recent Supreme Court cases that focus on the traditional purpose of trademark law, we instead argue that courts should be clear what they are doing when they endorse a brand right. By recognizing that brand rights are not like traditional trademark law, we can stop the distortions of trademark doctrine brand rights have introduced.  And we can think expressly about what a brand right should look like, freed from the cover of pretending that it is only a right to prevent consumer confusion. That will enable courts to set much-needed rules for establishing when such a right exists, how it might be infringed, and the limits that the First Amendment and other doctrines should place on a new property right to control an important means of communication.

title: Transparency and Stability in the Post-GENIUS Act Era: A Reserve Opacity Analysis of Dollar-Denominated Stablecoins
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Transparency and Stability in the Post-GENIUS Act Era: A Reserve Opacity Analysis of Dollar-Denominated Stablecoins
detail.abstract: The enactment of the GENIUS Act in July 2025 established the first comprehensive federal framework for U.S. stablecoin regulation, mandating reserve transparency through detailed asset composition disclosure, maturity profiling, and third-party attestations. However, the Act's jurisdictional limitations create a bifurcated market where offshore issuers operate under divergent transparency standards, generating a natural experiment in how reserve opacity affects market stability. This study conducts a cross-sectional reserve opacity analysis of six large U.S. dollarpegged stablecoins representing over $250 billion in market capitalization, combining a structured Opacity Scoring framework derived from GENIUS Act requirements and AICPA attestation criteria with high-frequency market data from September 1, 2025, through January 20, 2026. We identify a three-tier transparency hierarchy based on specific disclosure deficiencies rather than regulatory domicile alone. Our central finding is that reserve opacity and market illiquidity operate as multiplicative rather than additive risks, formalized through a novel Fragility Factor metric (Opacity ÷ Liquidity) that explains 74.4% of peg stability variance across issuers. Stablecoins with moderate opacity (Tier 2) in low-liquidity environments exhibit peg instability 3.9 times worse than fully transparent peers with similar liquidity profiles, constituting a "fragility trap." Conversely, high liquidity can create a "liquidity veneer" that is often driven by exchange-level subsidies rather than organic demand, which temporarily buffers normal-period volatility but fails under stress. An event study of the October 10, 2025 tariff-induced market crash validates that our transparency framework predicts crisis resilience, with Tier 1 issuers maintaining peak deviations below 10 basis points while opaque issuers experienced depegs exceeding 44 basis points. These findings demonstrate that markets price a substantial transparency premium and that incomplete reserve disclosures, particularly the absence of instrument-level maturity data, represent a latent systemic vulnerability in a $300+ billion ecosystem. We recommend mandatory global standards for maturity disclosure and liquidity-adjusted stress testing for systemically important stablecoin issuers.

title: Benchmark Index Inclusion and Sovereign Risk
affiliations: University of California, Davis, Department of Economics

detail.title: Benchmark Index Inclusion and Sovereign Risk
detail.abstract: Rising global capital flows intermediated by investment funds that replicate benchmark indicesthe returns of a basket of eligible assets-have raised financial stability concerns. I exploit variation in benchmarks used by investors holding bonds from the same issuer to estimate the causal effect of adding a country's debt to benchmark indices on bond price volatility. Using micro-level data on government debt from emerging economies, I show that index inclusion insulates bond prices from changes in fundamental risk, reducing volatility. On the borrower side, benchmark inclusion encourages borrowing as the level of demand for a country's bonds rises. However, the dampening effect of inclusion on the elasticity of demand for the bond has a countervailing impact. I develop and estimate a structural model with benchmark-driven demand and endogenous asset supply. The level effect on demand dominates, indicating that an increased supply of index-eligible assets contributes to volatility.

title: Arrow's Shadow over Climate Governance

detail.title: Arrow's Shadow over Climate Governance
detail.abstract: Thirty years of climate negotiations have not produced a stable, widely accepted rule for distributing mitigation burdens. Common explanations emphasize political will, free-riding, and domestic constraints. These factors are important, but they are insufficient to account for the persistent difficulty of burdensharing relative to other contested pillars, including technology transfer and adaptation finance. This paper argues that burden-sharing faces structural constraints illuminated by Arrow's impossibility theorem. Modeling negotiations as collective choice over candidate burden-sharing rules, the theorem suggests that no procedurally fair aggregation can yield a stable social ordering when parties hold heterogeneous, principled commitments to historical responsibility, capability, and equal per capita claims. The paper makes three linked contributions. First, it applies Arrow's theorem as a diagnostic for climate governance, clarifying what political conflict is about: which fairness criterion is implicitly relaxed to reach agreement. Second, it reframes issue linkage not as a negotiating tactic but as a deliberate relaxation of Arrow's independence condition; when the ranking of allocation approaches depends on what else is under consideration, as illustrated by disputes over agenda-setting and draft texts at Copenhagen, crossissue bundling makes that dependence explicit and negotiable. Third, it interprets the Paris Agreement's architecture as a rational response to aggregation failure: nationally determined contributions permit parties to act on divergent fairness rationales, while temperature goals coordinate expectations without requiring agreement on burden shares. This implies that renewed pushes for comprehensive allocation formulas should expect the same structural deadlock that constrained pre-Paris negotiations. Sen's comparative justice framework helps explain how incremental progress remains possible under impossibility; it also highlights that such progress depends on a shared evaluative frame grounded in the UNFCCC objective. When that frame is rejected, the basis for comparative judgment and iterative cooperation erodes.

title: Adaptive Market Ecology and Conditional Strategy Performance: Evidence from Machine-Learning Market-Timing Strategies
affiliations: Imperial College London, Imperial College London - Accounting, Finance, and Macroeconomics and

detail.title: Adaptive Market Ecology and Conditional Strategy Performance: Evidence from Machine-Learning Market-Timing Strategies
detail.abstract: We evaluate traditional and modern machine-learning market-timing strategies from 1970 to 2024 under a common information set, portfolio rule, and realistic transaction costs. Unconditionally, none of the strategies delivers robust abnormal performance relative to buy-andhold, consistent with the Efficient Markets Hypothesis (EMH). Conditioning on an ex-ante ecology vector capturing crowding, funding, liquidity, and volatility, performance, risk, and cross-strategy co-movement vary systematically, with different model families specializing in distinct habitats. These state-dependent patterns are difficult to reconcile with a purely riskbased EMH but align closely with the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis (AMH).

title: WP02 — The System Acceleration Model (Aₜ)

detail.title: WP02 — The System Acceleration Model (Aₜ)

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Modern economic systems no longer evolve at human speed. Over the past two decades, technology has transformed the structural tempo of markets, institutions, and societies, creating environments where systemic velocity repeatedly exceeds biological, cognitive, and institutional absorption limits. Existing macroeconomic frameworks—GDP-based models, DSGE structures, Taylor-rule derivatives, and Growth-at-Risk systems—implicitly assume that systemic change occurs within equilibrium temporal boundaries. Yet empirical evidence across financial markets, labor dynamics, digital ecosystems, and information networks shows that system acceleration has surpassed these boundaries.

This paper introduces Aₜ, the System Acceleration Model, as the first macro-temporal methodology for quantifying the rate of change in modern accelerated systems. Aₜ captures the compression of information cycles, decision cycles, coordination cycles, and innovation cycles—four core dimensions that collectively determine systemic velocity. We formalize Aₜ mathematically, decompose it into structural subcomponents, analyze non-linear acceleration behaviors, and examine the conditions under which Aₜ generates temporal misalignment, institutional lag amplification, and macro-instability. As the foundational variable underlying GHDP™ (Gross Human Dynamics Product) and Tempo Economics™, Aₜ provides a robust analytic framework for understanding how, why, and when systems exceed human and institutional tempo constraints. The findings suggest that central banks, regulators, and macroeconomic institutions must begin treating system acceleration as a first-order stability parameter rather than a background phenomenon.

title: Modeling Justice Without Deciding It

detail.title: Modeling Justice Without Deciding It
detail.abstract: Integrated assessment models (IAMs) are increasingly asked to incorporate equity and justice considerations. This development responds to valid criticism that earlier models ignored distribution. However, incorporating equity is not a technical upgrade analogous to improving model resolution. It requires ethical closure: substantive commitments about how to compare welfare across people, regions, and generations. Arrow's impossibility theorem identifies this requirement under ordinal information; subsequent work shows that escaping impossibility requires ethically loaded commitments about comparability and aggregation, while intergenerational results demonstrate that even then key desiderata conflict. This paper argues that IAM outputs are often used to answer a question they cannot answer in a framework-neutral way: which climate policies are preferable? Policy evaluation requires ethical closure; what fails is the claim to framework-independent authority. What IAMs can do is map consequences: given pathway X and ethical framework Y, here are the distributional outcomes. This reframing clarifies what models contribute to policy deliberation. Rather than delivering optimal policies, they illuminate trade-offs across normatively distinct scenarios. The implications extend to current initiatives: asking models to "include equity" without specifying which equity reproduces the closure problem; asking models to map implications of different equity frameworks is tractable and informative. The path forward requires treating justice assumptions as scenario dimensions comparable to Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, not as parameters buried in model code.

title: The Forensic Accounting: Advanced Techniques for Preventing Financial Fraud and Misstatements under Global Competition
affiliations: Brainae University, Province Government and Madhesh University

detail.title: The Forensic Accounting: Advanced Techniques for Preventing Financial Fraud and Misstatements under Global Competition
detail.abstract: Global competition needs to taken care of to avoid Financial Fraud and Misstatements. Forensic accounting has evolved significantly with the increasing complexity of financial fraud and corporate misstatements. This study explores how advanced forensic techniques-such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, data analytics, and predictive modeling-are transforming fraud detection and prevention. The research aims to assess the effectiveness of these methods, examine their role in corporate governance, and analyze their impact on regulatory compliance. A mixed-methods approach was employed, integrating empirical data analysis, case studies, and statistical modeling. The findings demonstrate a strong correlation (0.995) between AI adoption, blockchain technology, and forensic expertise in improving fraud detection efficiency. Regression analysis confirms that a 1% increase in AI adoption enhances fraud prevention by 0.92%, while blockchain integration reduces fraud by 0.76% per 1% increase. The results validate that forensic accounting significantly strengthens fraud detection, mitigates financial risks, and ensures corporate transparency. The study recommends broader AI implementation, enhanced forensic training.

detail.abstract: The data network is not only about collecting data from participants but also has a meaning in supporting sustainable development. Through analyzing common data on supply chains, product life cycles, and consumer behavior, the data network helps identify opportunities for green technology innovation and circular economic models. In the long term, the circular economy needs to build a data network to ensure that activities will be maintained in the most harmonious state. Based on the method of collecting information and analyzing secondary data, the article will review current Vietnamese legal policies and assess the current status of data governance in Vietnam. In addition, the study also analyzes the experiences of China and the European Union (EU). This provides some valuable lessons for Vietnam in the journey of perfecting the national data network, serving the development of the circular economy.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Cross-Sectional Equity Signals Under Backtest Overfitting Diagnostics
affiliations: Rutgers University, New Jersey

detail.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Cross-Sectional Equity Signals Under Backtest Overfitting Diagnostics
detail.abstract: This paper presents a large-scale empirical replication and diagnostic study of simple crosssectional equity return prediction signals using modern validation techniques designed to mitigate backtest overfitting. Using over 25 million U.S. equity stock-day observations, we implement interpretable momentum, reversal, and volume-based features commonly studied in the asset pricing literature. Model evaluation is conducted under Combinatorially Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV), and selection bias is quantified using the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO). While in-sample results suggest weak predictive structure, out-of-sample performance deteriorates substantially, with high turnover and a PBO estimate of approximately 0.60. Rather than proposing new signals or models, this study aims to illustrate how rigorous validation alters conclusions about the economic robustness of widely used cross-sectional strategies.

title: You Only Live Twice: Financial Inflows and Growth in a Westward-Facing Ukraine
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: You Only Live Twice: Financial Inflows and Growth in a Westward-Facing Ukraine
detail.abstract:
The monumental task of rebuilding postwar Ukraine requires early planning and identification of growth strategies. The earlier accession of Eastern European countries to the European Union and NATO offers a template that relies on massive foreign direct investment and public structural funds. This approach helps to raise incomes directly and can create a virtuous circle where capital deepening facilitates technological upgrades and repatriation of war refugees, which in turn stimulate more investment. We show theoretically that the government can refine this strategy by internalizing positive externalities from having a higher capital stock: Investment in physical capital relaxes borrowing constraints (thus allowing more capital inflows) and raises wages (thus encouraging more Ukrainian refugees to return home).

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the United States-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund Agreement of April 2025, examining its potential to redefine post-conflict reconstruction finance through an innovative equity-based partnership model. Unlike traditional foreign aid mechanisms relying on grants or sovereign lending, the Agreement establishes a co-governed limited partnership between the U.S. Development Finance Corporation and Ukraine's Agency on Support Public-Private Partnership, converting possible military assistance into capital contributions that may generate equity stakes in Ukraine's critical mineral extraction projects. The framework leverages Ukraine's estimated $12 trillion in natural resources as collateral for reconstruction financing while addressing U.S. strategic mineral security concerns. This article identifies three key mechanisms for analysis: transformation of military aid into deemed capital contributions, market-based investment rights, and offtake arrangements for critical minerals.

detail.title: The Public and Private Enforcement of EU Digital Space Private Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Review of Private Law, Vol. 33, Nos 5 & 6, pp. 1073-1102, 2025

detail.abstract: European Union (EU) digital space private law harnesses both public and private enforcement in the pursuit of its policy goals. This article explores whether this part of EU private law is supported by a coherent enforcement architecture and how this architecture could be improved so as to make effective use of public and private enforcement tools. It takes stock of the enforcement landscape across EU digital space private law, categorizing various EU measures according to their approach to enforcement and seeking to explain the differences between them. The article also examines what happens when the same rule can be enforced through both public and private law means, focusing on the interaction between the actors involved, notably regulatory agencies and administrative courts, on the one hand, and private law courts, on the other hand. This analysis highlights the lack of sufficient cross-area and crossactor coordination in enforcement matters, raising concerns about whether the EU's current enforcement policy for digital space private law is effective in preventing and remedying regulatory violations and whether it is in line with the EU law principles of effectiveness, proportionality, and dissuasiveness. The article concludes with a plea for a holistic approach to the public and private enforcement of EU digital space private law.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w34718
title: Structural Change and Jobless Development
affiliations: World Bank, Princeton University - Princeton School of Public and International Affairs and World Bank

detail.title: Structural Change and Jobless Development
detail.abstract:
Benchmark models of structural transformation focus on the reallocation of employment across sectors while assuming that overall employment stays constant. We show that this assumption does not match facts for developing economies. We study a panel of 48 mostly developing economies over the period 1990--2018 and document a strong positive relationship between the share of the population employed in agriculture and the overall employment rate. That is, the early part of the development process is associated with a substantial decline in the total employment rate. Motivated by this finding, we extend a benchmark model of structural change featuring Stone-Geary preferences to allow for endogenous labor supply. We show that this model can account for the patterns we document in the data both qualitatively and quantitatively. We use a calibrated version of our model to study the employment dynamics in several developing economies and show that structural change is a quantitatively important source of employment changes during the early stages of development.

title: Gender Norms and the Labor Market

detail.title: Gender Norms and the Labor Market
detail.abstract:
Despite substantial convergence in men’s and women’s economic roles, gender gaps in labor market outcomes persist across countries. This article provides a unified framework for understanding how gender norms shape economic behavior, distinguishing between internalized norms—preferences and beliefs tied to gender identity—and external norms arising from peer pressure and social coordination. We first document cross-country and within-country variation in gender attitudes, alongside gradual but uneven shifts toward more egalitarian views. We then review empirical evidence on the origins, persistence, and transmission of gender norms, and their effects on human capital accumulation, labor supply, wages, and policy take-up. The review highlights both the durability of gender norms and the mechanisms through which policies, institutions, and media can induce norm change, with implications for the design of effective interventions.

title: Financial Crises: History, Theory and New Insights

detail.title: Financial Crises: History, Theory and New Insights
detail.abstract:
This review essay discusses the history, causes and consequences of financial crises. In recent years scholars have assembled new sources of data and utilized new empirical designs to analyze crises, shedding light on old questions and producing new insights. This essay highlights those new insights, and uses the historical record of crises in the United States to put those insights into perspective. I begin with a discussion of the defining characteristics of financial crises and their evolution, both in the U.S. and in the rest of the world. I then revisit the chronology of crises in the U.S. since 1870. Data on bank failure rates and large-bank equity losses suggest that some panics were not full-blown financial crises, and also identify episodes when no panic occurred that could potentially be considered crises. I then turn to two categories of theoretical models developed to analyze the mechanisms responsible for crises. The first focuses on asset price bubbles, which have been associated with many crises. The second is focused on the dynamics of bank runs and panics, which have been especially common in the United States. Finally, I present an overview of the effects of crises and the mechanisms transmitting financial distress in the banking system into the rest of the economy.

detail.title: Modeling the Labor Implications of the Energy Transition
detail.abstract:
The energy transition away from fossil fuels toward alternative energy sources will, like every significant economic transition, disrupt existing economic relationships and markets. Disruption in the labor market is of particular concern due to the distributional and political importance of energy jobs and the potential concentration of risks on workers in carbon-intensive sectors and regions that are particularly reliant on fossil-fuel industries. We look at modeling the labor implications of the energy transition. We outline a conceptual framework for analyzing the labor-market risks, focusing on obstacles to labor-market adjustments during the transition. We then review empirical research on such barriers to labor-market adjustments, with a focus on evidence that can inform modeling efforts. We also survey the literature on ex-ante modeling of the effects of the energy transition on labor markets, identifying both the challenges and opportunities for new research in this field.

title: Speculative Growth and the AI "Bubble"
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Speculative Growth and the AI "Bubble"
detail.abstract:
AI technology can generate speculative-growth equilibria. These are rational but fragile: elevated valuations support rapid capital accumulation, yet persist only as long as beliefs remain coordinated. Because AI capital is labor-like, it expands effective labor and dampens the normal decline in the marginal product of capital as the capital stock grows. The gains from this expansion accrue disproportionately to capitalists, whose saving rate rises with wealth, raising aggregate saving. Building on Caballero et al (2006), I show that these features generate a funding feedback—rising capitalist wealth lowers the required return—that can produce multiple equilibria. With intermediate adjustment costs, elevated valuations are the mechanism that sustains a transition toward a high-capital equilibrium; a loss of confidence can precipitate a self-fulfilling crash and reversal.

detail.abstract: This study's central question is: how does the internet impact political participation and democracy? The internet has reconfigured the dynamics of democracy, enabling more direct dialogue between representatives and civil society. It also imposes new challenges, particularly regarding the limits of digital platform usage and their increasing appropriation for illicit purposes. Given this scenario, this article analyzes the complex relationship between the internet, regulation, and democracy, emphasizing the role of digital platforms in political participation and the emerging regulatory challenges. For this purpose, besides the introduction and concluding remarks, this study also has five sections: the first contextualizes the intersection of democracy, participation, and the internet; the second addresses the phenomenon of cyberactivism and digital social movements, analyzing their potentialities and limitations; the third delves deeper into themes such as control, access to information, and the participatory pathways enabled by digital media; the fourth discusses aspects of internet regulation and governance, with a comparison between the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Brazil's proposed Fake News Bill (PL 2630/2020); and the fifth examines empirical challenges to digital democracy by analyzing concrete cases of online manipulation and disinformation and discussing the urgent need for more robust regulatory responses. The concluding remarks point to a scenario of increasing tension between state regulation and the resistance of digital platforms to complying with judicial orders, highlighting a new chapter in this complex relationship and prompting reflections on the future of democracy in the digital age.

detail.title: Migration and the Making of the English Middle Class
detail.abstract:
When do people identify with their class? Evidence from social psychology shows that individuals are more likely to identify with a group if they are similar to its members. We study early 20th century Britain and show that regional cultural heterogeneity combined with internal migration influenced class identity. We develop and validate a measure of class identity using naming decisions. Exploiting within-household variation, we show that migration patterns that increased the local share of culturally-distant workers reduced working class identification. Where migration increased the cultural distance of the working class, workers were less likely to join unions, voters were less likely to support the nascent Labour Party, and parliamentary candidates were less likely to target working class voters. By 1911, slower in-migration and rising local population growth reduced working class distance in urban areas, which also became strongholds of support for Labour. Migration alters social identity and creates political cleavages.

detail.title: The Contribution of College Majors to Gender and Racial Earnings Differences
detail.abstract:
Gender and racial/ethnic gaps in labor market earnings remain large, even among college-goers. Cross-gender and race/ethnic differences in choice of and returns to college major are potentially important contributors. Following Texas public high school graduates for up to 20 years through college and the labor market, we assess gender and racial differences in college major choices and the consequences of these choices. Women and underrepresented minorities are less likely than men, Whites, and Asians to major in high earning fields like business, economics, engineering, and computer science, however we also show that they experience lower returns to these majors. Differences in major-specific returns relative to liberal arts explain about one quarter of the gender, White-Black, and White-Hispanic (but not White-Asian) earnings gaps among four-year college students and become larger contributors to earnings gaps than differential major distributions as workers age. We present suggestive evidence that differences in occupation choices within field are a key driver of the differences in returns across groups. The work shines light on the roles that college major choice and returns by gender and race contribute to inequality.

detail.title: Missing Black Men? The Impact of Non-Reporting on Estimates of Labor Market Outcomes for Black Men
detail.abstract:
Adult Black men persistently do not report to household-based surveys, with demographers estimating non-reporting rates of 7-14% from 1970-2020. We derive a method to account for incomplete data and show that non-reporting rates are up to 5.5 percentage points (pp) larger than prior estimates, with significant heterogeneity by year. We then show that Black men at risk of incarceration drive non-reporting. We use state-year variation in incarceration rates to estimate that 35-83% of the incarcerated population would have been non-reporting if not incarcerated. Adjusting for previously uncorrected non-reporting shows that the Black-white gap in high-school completion is 20-39% (3.0-5.9 pp) larger, college attendance is 8-18% (3.1-6.1 pp) larger, and earnings is 10-20% (2.8-5.7 pp) larger. In contrast, the gap in employment is 4-8% (0.6-1.6 pp) smaller than previously thought.

detail.title: Senior Migration, Local Economic Development and Spatial Concentration
detail.abstract:
We document that migration flows upon retirement are predominantly from richer, more urban to poorer, more rural regions. In theory, the local economic implications of senior in-migration are ambiguous, while empirically there is little existing evidence on whether attracting mobile seniors can be an effective tool to promote economic development among lagging regions. We combine a unique collection of microdata from France with a new empirical strategy to fill this gap. We find that senior inflows have significant positive effects on the local economy over the course of a decade, including increases in the working-age population, total employment, GDP, average incomes, fiscal revenues and housing construction. These effects are particularly pronounced among initially poorer regions. They are accompanied by an increase in the share of services in the local economy, driven by employment growth in health, food services and retail sectors. Combining these estimates with observed region-to-region net migration flows, we find that mobile seniors have become a significant force for reducing the concentration of employment and GDP across regions.

detail.title: Rational Disagreement
detail.abstract:
We propose rational disagreement as a formal framework for analyzing seemingly irrational behavior that can persist despite the wide availability of objective information in a steady-state. Agents are rational in that they correctly anticipate the distribution of aggregate outcomes, yet disagree about which specific individuals perform better than others. Notably, the subjective belief of any individual may be objectively correct. We illustrate the key concepts with a simple entry game. We show how unordered individual outcome distributions can be identified solely from aggregate statistics. We then characterize the resulting game, define its Nash equilibria, and develop a statistical test for the null hypothesis of agreement. Finally, we situate our framework within the broader literature on Bayesian games, behavioral biases, and the rational expectations hypothesis.

detail.title: No Taxation Without Administration: Bringing The State Back Into The Public Finance Of Developing Countries
detail.abstract:
The empirical economics literature on taxation in developing countries has centered on the importance of third-party information for enforcement. Yet, while surely a long-run objective, leveraging such information remains out of reach in many developing countries due to largely informal economies and low state capacity. This article examines an emerging complementary literature focused on strengthening the 'sinews' of state capacity: tax administration. We argue that reforms to the organizational structure, personnel management, and task management of tax authorities have potential to raise tax capacity in developing countries. We also argue that efforts to improve the state's legitimacy – popular acceptance of its right to tax – can increase capacity and may complement investments in tax administration. Our approach bridges a long-standing divide between how scholars in public finance and political economy approach tax capacity building in developing countries.

detail.title: Technology and Economic Development
detail.abstract:
This chapter presents a tractable framework for the study of technology adoption and diffusion in the context of economic development. Firms in countries behind the world technology frontier can rapidly adopt new techniques from the world frontier. Lower absorptive capacity (because of weak education systems, poor management practices, or barriers to technology adoption), institutional distortions, mismatch between frontier technologies and the needs of firms in the country (i.e., “inappropriate technology”), and credit market frictions slow down technology adoption and cause the economy in question to have a greater distance to the frontier and thus lower income per capita—although the long-run growth rate of the country still remains equal to that of the frontier. This framework is extended to study the choice between innovation and imitation, as well as the role of selection for higher-productivity and higher-absorptive capacity firms during the process of economic development. We illustrate the main comparative statics of our framework with a number of correlations based on cross-country and firm-level data. The tractability of the framework makes it amenable to a range of additional extensions.

title: Global Trade, Tariff Uncertainty and the U.S. Dollar
affiliations: Brown University, Brown University and Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS)

detail.title: Global Trade, Tariff Uncertainty and the U.S. Dollar
detail.abstract:
We analyze how tariff uncertainty affects exchange rates, motivated by the U.S. dollar’s depreciation after the 2025 tariff announcements. Standard macro-trade models predict that unilateral tariffs appreciate the implementing country’s currency, but we show this result can be overturned by policy uncertainty. We build a two-country general equilibrium model with risk-averse agents and segmented financial markets, where tariff volatility enters uncovered interest parity through a risk-premium wedge. Higher tariff uncertainty increases precautionary savings and risk premia, leading to immediate currency depreciation even as tariffs rise. Quantitatively, the model replicates the size and timing of the observed dollar depreciation episode dynamics.
