title: Market Manipulation vs. Psychological Barriers: Unraveling the Causes of Market Crashes and Future Trends in Bangladesh Stock Market
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Dhaka and

detail.title: Market Manipulation vs. Psychological Barriers: Unraveling the Causes of Market Crashes and Future Trends in Bangladesh Stock Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bangladesh Students' Digest on Economics & Development, Volume 6, No. 1, Pp. 9-26

detail.abstract: Two significant stock market crashes have left millions of individuals financially devastated and have instilled a widespread panic about investing in the stock market. While market manipulation played a crucial role in the formation of speculative bubbles, it was not the sole factor. Psychological biases influencing speculative entry and panic-driven exits during the burst phase also significantly contributed to market instability. This study examines various market manipulation tactics observed during the 1996 and 2011 stock market crashes and analyzes the psychological factors that influenced investors' decisions before entering and exiting the market. By utilizing primary data from surveys conducted among well-informed and educated potential investors, this research seeks to determine whether, in the event of another market manipulation, the stock market would experience another severe crash.

title: Market System to Curtail Emission Magnitudes Evolved from Electricity Generation
affiliations: Dr. Momtaz Begum University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Market System to Curtail Emission Magnitudes Evolved from Electricity Generation
detail.abstract: The recent resolution of the seventh Conference of the Parties to the Climate Convention (COP7) indicates that if a country is required to comply with the pollution limit, part of the required reduction in levels of emission will have to be achieved domestically. With this status quo, policy practitioners may opt to design emission level standards along with the provision of allowing access to the international permit market that may facilitate carbon offset crediting to the country. In policy formulation cognate to electricity generation through coal combustion, it is suggested that end-users will pay emission compliance costs in terms of the price of electricity usage and the companies will offer a rebate on reduction to those who curtail the level of usage of electricity. Under the scheme proposed, the generating company(s) will face the consequences if it fails to comply to domestic emission standards. In practice, the proposed method can ensure 'Pareto efficiency' and exhibit 'Pareto improvement' in two-party cases where both parties have joint interest in profit maximization, but they may have dichotomy in their activities. In dealing with domestic greenhouse gas issues, the proposal becomes appealing to parties for reducing the level of emissions. Moreover, it may produce a greater degree of abatement of CO 2 emissions over the levels of abatement resulting from policies of consumer or producer liability assignments.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w34731
title: Salience and the Elasticity of Taxable Income: Evidence from Top-bracket Tax Reforms
affiliations: HEC Montreal, HEC Montreal and University of Toronto

detail.title: Salience and the Elasticity of Taxable Income: Evidence from Top-bracket Tax Reforms
detail.abstract:
We estimate heterogeneous responses to top-bracket tax reforms using a triple-difference design that exploits variation in tax rate changes and the thresholds at which they apply. This strategy identifies behavioral responses even in the presence of unobservable shocks to the income distribution. Higher-income taxpayers respond more to top-rate changes, but our results indicate that this reflects the salience of the reforms—the larger mechanical change in average tax rates at higher incomes—rather than heterogeneity in substitution elasticities. We discuss implications for the revenue and distributional effects of top-bracket tax reforms.

title: Asking a Chatbot: The Effect of Conversational versus Static AI Interfaces on Belief Updating
affiliations: Tilburg University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Asking a Chatbot: The Effect of Conversational versus Static AI Interfaces on Belief Updating

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The experiment received approval from the Institutional Review Board of Tilburg University (application IRB EXE 2024-022). The study involved no deception.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by funding from CentERlab at Tilburg University.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of a conversational versus static interface for generative AI on belief updating. In a controlled laboratory experiment, participants reported incentivized beliefs about the correct answers to a series of multiple-choice reasoning questions both before and after receiving recommendations from the same AI model. For each question, in the conversational treatment, participants submitted a single query to a chatbot, which generated a recommendation consisting of an answer option and a brief justification in real time. In the static treatment, participants received a pre-generated recommendation presented in a fixed format. The informational content of AI-generated recommendations was distributionally matched across treatments. Belief updating was measured as the change in the belief that participants assigned to the AI-recommended option. On average, participants using the conversational interface increased their belief in the AI-recommended option by 31.75 percentage points, compared to 26.31 percentage points in the static treatment (p = 0.068). Exploratory analysis reveals that this average effect conceals a systematic heterogeneity: the effect is most pronounced when initial beliefs in the AI-recommended option conflict with the recommendation; it diminishes to near zero when initial beliefs and recommendations are aligned.

reference: İstanbul Hukuk Mecmuası / Istanbul Law Review, volume 83, issue 2, 2025[10.26650/mecmua.2025.83.2.0011]
title: The Effect of New Technologies on the Structure and Decision-Making Process of Multinational Enterprises and Their Liability for Human Rights and Environmental Breaches
affiliations: Boğaziçi University

detail.title: The Effect of New Technologies on the Structure and Decision-Making Process of Multinational Enterprises and Their Liability for Human Rights and Environmental Breaches

publicationDetails.detailsText: İstanbul Hukuk Mecmuası / Istanbul Law Review, volume 83, issue 2, 2025[10.26650/mecmua.2025.83.2.0011]

detail.abstract: Multinational enterprises (MNEs) are at the centre of international business activities and play an important role in the world economy's positive developments. However, they have long been accused of violating human rights and environmental regulations that harm people and societies. Several efforts have been made to solve the problems and make MNEs accountable and liable for their harmful actions. MNEs operate on a group-based managerial structure, while each constituent company within a group is subjected to local company laws and other regulations. This complicated internal structure has made it very difficult to establish the overall group liability for the torts of companies within the group. Although the legal structure based on company law has not changed for a long time, the internal structure decision-making processes within MNEs are undergoing a considerable transformation with the recent technological developments, such as big data, artificial intelligence, and distributed ledger technologies. Most recent case law and regulatory options regarding the liability of MNEs still consider them with their dated structure. This approach prevents victims of MNE adverse actions from reaching satisfactory solutions. The effects of new technologies must be considered while discussing any legal actions and introducing regulations towards accountability and liability of MNEs for their human rights and environmental breaches. This article provides an extensive analysis of the effects of new technologies on contemporary internal operations and the structure of MNEs, provides examples of current human rights and environmental violations, and discusses the suitability of current laws and regulations for solving liability problems.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the US Economy: An Accounting Perspective on Investment and Production
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Banca d’Italia

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the US Economy: An Accounting Perspective on Investment and Production
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved to the center of policy, market, and academic debates, but its macroeconomic footprint is still only partly understood. This paper provides an overview on how the current AI wave is captured in US national accounts, combining a simple macro-accounting framework with a stylized description of the AI production process. We highlight the crucial role played by data centers, which constitute the backbone of the AI ecosystem and have attracted formidable investment in 2025, as they are indispensable for meeting the rapidly increasing worldwide demand for AI services. We document that the boom in IT and AI-related capital expenditure in the first three quarters of the year has given an outsized boost to aggregate demand, while its contribution to GDP growth is smaller once the high import content of AI hardware is netted out. Furthermore, simple calculations suggest that, at current utilization rates and pricing, the production of services originating in new AI data centers could contribute to GDP over the turn of the next quarters on a scale comparable to that of investment spending to date. Short reinvestment cycles and uncertainty about future AI demand-while not currently acting as a macroeconomic drag-can nevertheless fuel macroeconomic risks over the medium term.

title: A Scenario Tool for Sustainability Transformation in Fisheries and Beyond
affiliations: Christian-Albrechts-University Kiel - Faculty of Agricultural and Nutritional Sciences & Center for Ocean and Society, Christian Albrechts-University of Kiel, University of Hamburg, Kiel Institute for the World Economy - IFW, University of Kiel - Faculty of Agriculture and Kiel University, Center for Ocean and Society

detail.title: A Scenario Tool for Sustainability Transformation in Fisheries and Beyond
detail.abstract: The urgency to find sustainable management solutions intensifies with increasing natural resource scarcity. Resource sectors are usually characterized by diverse resource users. We developed a structured scenario tool designed to quantitatively assess policy options for achieving sustainability, accounting for ecological, economic and institutional boundaries. Parameterized with stakeholders' input, the tool is exemplified for the German Western Baltic fishery, a sector under pressure from collapsing fish stocks and often regarded as "time machine". It fits the structure of many resource sectors with different user types, often few large and many small-scale users. We evaluate two ecological scenarios in combination with four governance approaches against the economic viability of different fishery types. Under low biological productivity, the current quota allocation is not economically viable for most fishery types, highlighting how environmental crises leads to human crises. While large-scale fisheries stay unsustainable in the Western Baltic, a quota redistribution could pave the way for viable small-scale fisheries. The tool illustrates interrelations between boundaries to support evidencebased policy-making for sustainability transformations in fisheries, but also for allocations of land use, emissions or water rights. It also illustrates the role of firms' cost structures for economic viability when ecological boundaries require reduced natural resource use and how institutional settings can support a sustainable natural resource sector.

title: Do Declines in Labor Market Fluidity Cause Productivity Slowdown?
affiliations: University of Montreal - Université de Montreal

detail.title: Do Declines in Labor Market Fluidity Cause Productivity Slowdown?
detail.abstract: Productivity growth is closely related to worker mobility when firms are heterogeneous in levels and growth rates of productivity. Using a Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides model of labor market frictions augmented with innovation, I quantify the impact of labor market trends on productivity slowdown after the 2000s. Four labor market trends are put into the model: lower birth, job destruction, and start-up rates, and lower matching efficiency. The calibrated model shows that decreased matching efficiency and job destruction rates are more detrimental to incumbent innovation and growth than slow population growth and lower start-up rates after the 2000s.

title: Non-Competes, Worker Mobility, and Productivity Growth: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: University of Montreal - Université de Montreal

detail.title: Non-Competes, Worker Mobility, and Productivity Growth: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that increased worker mobility between employers promotes innovation and accelerates growth. In the US, metropolitan areas subject to state-level court rulings that reduced the enforceability of non-compete (NC) clauses experienced increases in employment-to-employment (EE) hire rates. These areas also produced higher-quality patents and achieved faster productivity growth. Motivated by these empirical results, this paper develops an endogenous growth model with a frictional labor market and worker-embodied knowledge that increases innovation efficiency. Accelerated knowledge flows associated with EE transitions increase innovation and growth. The calibrated model shows that a permanent ban on NC clauses raises the annual growth rate by 0.2-0.3 percentage points, and the effect strengthens over time. Without the knowledge channel, the increase in growth rate is underestimated by more than 50%.

title: Spatial Distribution of Housing Liquidity
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department Finance,  and Kiel Institute for the World Economy - IFW

detail.title: Spatial Distribution of Housing Liquidity
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between location, liquidity, and prices in housing markets. We construct spatial datasets for German and U.S. cities and show that liquidity and prices decline with distance to the city center. To rationalize these patterns, we develop a spatial model of housing search. Location preferences concentrate buyers in central areas, generating tighter markets that are more liquid and command higher prices. Counterfactuals show that increasing search efficiency raises welfare and prices, especially in peripheral areas. Our findings highlight the importance of demand-side preferences and market tightness for understanding liquidity and asset prices.

title: Does Large Language Models have Market Timing Ability? Evidence from Global Markets
affiliations: Hunan University - College of Finance and Statistics, Hunan University - School of Finance and Statistics and Guangdong University of Finance & Economics

detail.title: Does Large Language Models have Market Timing Ability? Evidence from Global Markets

declarations.ethicsApproval: National Natural Science Foundation of China (72573052); Ministry of Education Humanities and Social Sciences (24YJC790159, 25YJC790160); Natural Science Foundation of Hunan Province, China (2025JJ50425); Guangdong Philosophy and Social Science Foundation (GD25YYJ37); Guangdong University Featured Innovation Program Project (2025WTSCX029)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the market timing ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in predicting global stock returns, using a large-scale dataset of daily market returns from 30 countries spanning from 2000 to 2024. The analysis focuses on assessing whether LLMs, when trained on past return sequences, can provide economically meaningful predictions of future market movements. Our results show that LLMs exhibit limited market-timing ability, with incremental returns often close to zero or even negative in developed markets, and positive but infrequent in emerging markets. We also find that the LLMs' performance is constrained by behavioral biases, including salience-driven decision-making, which mimics human cognitive processes. Specifically, we show that the models' forecasting accuracy is higher when market returns exhibit greater salience or predictable patterns. Our findings contribute to the literature on machine learning in finance by highlighting the limitations of LLMs in market timing and the role of behavioral biases in their decision-making processes.

title: Interpreting Firm Characteristic Behaviors in Machine Learning Asset Pricing Models
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology - School of Business, Stevens Institute of Technology - School of Business and

detail.title: Interpreting Firm Characteristic Behaviors in Machine Learning Asset Pricing Models
detail.abstract: This study proposes a model-agnostic framework to interpret how firm characteristics enter machine-learning asset-pricing models. Using Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), we generate local surrogate explanations by perturbing the input for individual firm-time predictions and then aggregate these local sensitivities into global statistical inference. We classify each characteristic's predictive role into economically interpretable behaviors-linearity, independence, insignificance, and interaction-thereby shifting attention from "which predictors matter" to "how predictors matter". We find that characteristic behaviors are heterogeneous and frequently conditional: interaction effects are pervasive and often account for predictive content that would be understated or missed by linear and additive analyses. These results challenge the traditional emphasis on stable linear and independent effects in characteristic-based asset pricing and clarify why flexible machine-learning models can outperform linear benchmarks. Overall, our framework provides a transparent and portable interpretability layer that can be applied to a wide range of machine-learning models, enabling fair comparisons across algorithms and offering a bridge between explainable AI tools and economic questions in empirical asset pricing.

title: An Evaluation of Social Security Reforms: Policy Substitution and Redistributive Consequences *
affiliations: Georgia State University - Andrew Young School of Policy Studies and

detail.title: An Evaluation of Social Security Reforms: Policy Substitution and Redistributive Consequences *
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the effects of Social Security (SS) reforms, incorporating its interactions with Disability Insurance (DI). The 1983 Social Security Amendments, by raising the full retirement age and increasing early claiming penalties, made DI relatively more generous compared to early SS claiming. We provide empirical evidence that this shift in relative generosity induced individuals to substitute early SS claiming for DI enrollment. To quantify its implications, we estimate a life-cycle model and find that the DI program significantly mitigates the reform's regressive fiscal and welfare impacts, particularly for individuals in poor health, by serving as a critical safety net.

title: Childhood Adversity and Adult Depression: Evidence from Self-Employed and Salaried Workers
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Industrial & Systems Engineering and Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: Childhood Adversity and Adult Depression: Evidence from Self-Employed and Salaried Workers
detail.abstract: This study examines whether the association between childhood adversity and adult depression differs between self-employed individuals and salaried workers. Using longitudinal survey data, we assess three forms of childhood adversity, namely material deprivation, threat exposure, and emotional deprivation, and show that each is positively associated with adult depression. Although self-employment has no direct association with depression, it strengthens the relationship between childhood material deprivation and depression. We further find that perceived control weakens this association among self-employed individuals. These results reveal heterogeneous patterns in how early-life adversity relates to mental health across work contexts and individual psychological resources, suggesting that self-employment may intensify, rather than mitigate, the emotional consequences of childhood material hardship.

title: Liberalisation and Protection under Overlapping Free Trade Agreements: Dynamic Interplay between Free Trade Agreements and Investment
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of International Development

detail.title: Liberalisation and Protection under Overlapping Free Trade Agreements: Dynamic Interplay between Free Trade Agreements and Investment
detail.abstract: Two decades into the most recent wave of regionalism many of its implications remain to be fully understood. A vast literature has explored the impacts of free trade agreements (FTAs) on investment flows, but less attention has been given to how existing patterns of investment alter FTA liberalisation. It is contended here that the dynamic interplay between overlapping FTA areas and the investment sunk in them shapes governments' and firms' positions regarding further FTA liberalisation. During trade negotiations, a country may decide to exclude a sector from FTA liberalisation to prevent (concession prevention) future FTA partners from making similar demands. Concession prevention could also occur when a foreign firm, holding a dominant market position in a host country, relinquishes liberalisation demands in an FTA between host and home countries to prevent its current position being eroded if the host country grants similar (or better) concessions to competing firms from other countries in future FTAs. Conversely, investment sunk into a country's sensitive sector in the territory of partners from previous FTAs could pre-empt (concession pre-emption) the protectionist position of that country when it subsequently negotiates FTAs with the investment-source countries. These arguments were tested in the negotiations around the liberalisation of the automotive industry that Thailand and Malaysia had with Japan in their respective bilateral FTAs. The distinct interaction between investment and the FTAs in which these countries participate resulted either in entrenchment of protectionism in the sector or its liberalisation across subsequent FTAs.

title: E-Business and Intellectual Property Rights (IPR): Policy, Practice, and Pathways for Trade and Business Growth in the Digital Economy

detail.title: E-Business and Intellectual Property Rights (IPR): Policy, Practice, and Pathways for Trade and Business Growth in the Digital Economy
detail.abstract: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) have become central to value creation in the digital economy, where intangibles such as data, software, brands, and designs dominate competitive advantage. As Indian trade and commerce digitize, firms face intersecting challenges in copyright, trademarks and domain names, trade secrets, data protection, competition law, and the patentability of computer-related inventions. This article synthesizes current developments-drawing on WIPO statistics, OECD digital economy outlooks, India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) and Rules (2025), evolving jurisprudence on "business method" exclusions, and the Competition Commission of India's focus on digital markets. It sets out a practical roadmap for businesses-especially MSMEs-to build IPR-ready e-business models that are compliant, innovation-friendly, and export-oriented. Policy recommendations emphasize coordinated IPR-competition-data governance, scale-up of MSME IP facilitation, and targeted reforms for trade secret protection and computer-related inventions.

reference: FEDS Notes No. 2026-01-07
title: Assessing Recession Risks with State-Level Data
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Department of Economics, Korea University and Independent

detail.title: Assessing Recession Risks with State-Level Data

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This note evaluates recession risks at the national and state levels using a state-of-the-art Bayesian Markov-switching model that distinguishes between full-recovery recessions (U-shaped recessions) and those that generate lasting damage, or hysteresis (L-shaped recessions). While states exhibit considerable heterogeneity in their business-cycle experiences, most saw some degree of hysteresis in the past recessions that occurred prior to the COVID pandemic. By contrast, the model classifies the pandemic-induced recession as a full-recovery episode with a low likelihood of hysteresis, reflecting the rapid rebound from the sharp downturn. The model suggests that the risk of a national recession has been low of late, though the state-level data reveal pockets of risk.

title: Preventing Silent Semantics Drift in Automated Trading Systems: Pre-Run Self-Checks and Runtime Guards Validated by Semantic Fault Injection
affiliations: Guangzhou College of Commerce

detail.title: Preventing Silent Semantics Drift in Automated Trading Systems: Pre-Run Self-Checks and Runtime Guards Validated by Semantic Fault Injection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants or personal data were involved; ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Operational failures of automated decision systems are often driven by silent semantic drift and misconfiguration rather than by modeling errors: evaluation semantics may change (e.g., T +0 vs. T +1), cost profiles may be unpinned, and risk limits may remain implicit until losses accumulate. We present a lightweight assurance layer that makes these controls explicit, executable, and auditable. The system has two components grounded in operational code: (i) a pre-run Self-Check that enforces strict semantic invariants (e.g., STRICT T +1 enabled, cost profile explicitly pinned, import provenance verified) and emits a semantic signature for traceability; and (ii) a post-deploy Live Guard that monitors realized trade logs, computes live risk/performance metrics, and triggers ok/watch/kill decisions with human-readable reasons (kill-switch signal when hard limits are breached). We validate the assurance layer with semantic fault injection: by injecting configuration faults into the Self-Check context and injecting adverse trade sequences into the Live Guard inputs, we show that the safeguards deterministically detect these injected violations and produce explainable decisions without relying on unverifiable profit claims. To reduce strawman comparisons, we also report two simple baselines (no-safeguard and a minimal baseline) on the same injected cases. To partially mitigate the limitation of purely synthetic traces, we also include a small price-conditioned stress test driven by repository-bundled OHLCV snapshots. Across the paper-scoped injected fault set, the safeguard matches the expected outcomes for all cases, and the in-process overhead is millisecond-scale. The result is an offline-reproducible assurance mechanism that helps detect “silent semantics drift” and provides a concrete evidence trail for review, regression checks, and incident response.

title: Music Sampling Law as Regulatory Vacuum and Check on Black Cultural Power
affiliations: American University - School of Communication

detail.title: Music Sampling Law as Regulatory Vacuum and Check on Black Cultural Power
detail.abstract: In this chapter, I discuss the "regulatory vacuum" surrounding music sampling in the United States as a strategic effort aimed at blunting the socially and institutionally disruptive power of Black aesthetics, intended to disproportionately silence Black voices and punish Black artists. After half a century of hip-hop, endless reinventions of popular music aesthetics, and the wholesale digitization of music production, distribution, promotion, and reception, U.S. copyright law has still failed to grapple with sampling as an art form. Instead, Congress has tacitly delegated this task to the courts, which have developed a large, complex, and often contradictory body of caselaw attempting to thread the needle between outlawing sampling and permitting it wholecloth. In other words, by refusing to deem sampling either legal or illegal, the U.S. legislature has created enough "wiggle room" to police the practice when it's used by minoritized actors in ways that challenge the hegemonic structures of Modernity and American empire, and to turn a blind eye when it's used in ways that conform to, or amplify, dominant ideologies. I conclude with some reflections on generative AI, the recent rise of racist, ultra-right wing politics, and the likely legal approach to creative reappropriation in the post-sampling era.

title: Behavioral Economics: Integrating Psychology and Mathematics into Economic Analysis

detail.title: Behavioral Economics: Integrating Psychology and Mathematics into Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: Behavioral economics, thanks to contributions from the science of Psychology, has progressively transformed economics itself, moving it from a theory based on extreme rationality proposed by classical and neoclassical economists to a science of human behavior. This article traces its intellectual evolution, beginning with the moral philosophy of Adam Smith and David Hume, continuing with the "old" behavioral programs of Herbert Simon and George Katona, and culminating in the "new" behavioral revolution led mainly by Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky, Richard Thaler, Vernon Smith, and Robert Shiller. Drawing on both historical and analytical perspectives, it attempts to build a dialogue between psychology and economics, to understand the methodological variations that shaped this field and how we see its expansion today, from individual and social knowledge to finance and public policy. This article concludes that this recent branch of economics now provides a more realistic microeconomic foundation for understanding choices, institutions, and collective welfare.

title: Cybersecurity Risk and Corporate Leverage Policies
affiliations: Sukkur IBA University, University of York, King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM) and

detail.title: Cybersecurity Risk and Corporate Leverage Policies
detail.abstract: Cyber-attacks impose financial losses, reputational damage, and customer distrust, yet little is known about how such risks alter firms' financing choices and capital structure decisions. While firms usually cut debt and conserve liquidity under uncertainty, cyber threats demand urgent investment in defensive technologies. Using a sample of 4,033 U.S. publicly listed companies from 2007 to 2018, this study examines how cybersecurity risk affects corporate financing policies. Results show that higher cybersecurity risk leads to increased book leverage and decreased market leverage, as firms raise debt to fund preventive measures while equity values decline due to increased investor risk perceptions. The effect is more pronounced among financially constrained firms and during non-crisis periods. Channel analysis suggests that cybersecurity risk prompts firms to increase leverage when facing financial distress, preferring debt over equity, extending debt maturities, and managing earnings volatility. These findings highlight the importance of integrating cybersecurity into capital structure decisions. Moreover, rising leverage in response to cyber threats may increase bankruptcy risk and, if left unaddressed, could contribute to broader financial instability. Policymakers should incorporate cyber risk into financial oversight by enforcing disclosure requirements, conducting cyber stress tests, and monitoring leverage adjustments, thereby strengthening resilience against systemic vulnerabilities.

title: Air Pollution Regimes and Green Bond Market Integration
affiliations: Chiang Mai University - Faculty of Business Administration, Chiang Mai University Business School, Chiang Mai University and Chiang Mai University Business School

detail.title: Air Pollution Regimes and Green Bond Market Integration
detail.abstract: This study examines whether air pollution regimes influence the dependence between green bond returns and major asset classes. Using a wavelet-based quantile-on-quantile framework, we analyze the Thai Green Bond index to capture nonlinear and horizon-specific dependence with the S&P 500, gold, Bitcoin, and domestic ESG equities under different air quality states. The results reveal that high-pollution regimes systematically amplify cross-market dependence, particularly in the upper tails, indicating that environmental stress strengthens the transmission of shocks from risky assets to green bonds. This state-dependent pattern is most pronounced for global equities and Bitcoin, while domestic ESG equities exhibit deeper long-horizon integration under poor air quality. These findings identify an environmental amplification channel in sustainable fixed-income markets and demonstrate that the diversification and hedging properties of green bonds vary significantly with environmental conditions. This study highlights the relevance of air quality as an additional state variable in portfolio allocation, risk management, and the design of a sustainable financial framework.

title: Yield-Based Allocation Among Stocks, Bonds, and Cash
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Yield-Based Allocation Among Stocks, Bonds, and Cash
detail.abstract: A portfolio that adequately balances earning potential against volatility enhances a retiree's spending flexibility and peace of mind. A "yield-based asset ratio" strategy for dynamic allocation between the S&P 500 stock index and ten-year US Treasury bonds on the basis of their yields would have delivered an overall return since 1911 that is comparable to that of a 100% stock portfolio, generally delivering equal or greater risk-adjusted return relative to 30%, 60%, and 100% static stock allocations. However, limiting fixed-income assets to include only bonds proved unfavorable when interest rates rose dramatically from near zero levels in 2022. If this had been mitigated by incrementally substituting "cash" (e.g., money market funds) for fixed-income assets as interest rates fell, the decline in portfolio value during 2022 would have been halved. Such an extended strategy would have had minimally impacted returns prior to 2008.

title: Environmental and Ecological Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers in the People's Republic of China: An International Comparative Perspective
affiliations: Peking University Beijing China and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: Environmental and Ecological Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers in the People's Republic of China: An International Comparative Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper explores the design, implementation, and impact of intergovernmental fiscal transfers aimed at environmental protection and ecological conservation in the People’s Republic of China (PRC). It provides a conceptual overview of conditional fiscal transfers—both traditional and output-based—and examines how these mechanisms are used to align national and local priorities for environmental quality. The study offers a detailed analysis of China’s central-local fiscal transfer system, highlighting the structure, allocation, and objectives of environmental and ecological transfers, and compares China’s approach with international experiences from countries such as Brazil, France, India, Indonesia, and Portugal. The paper concludes by discussing the strengths and limitations of China’s system, emphasizing its performance-oriented grants and the lessons it may offer for global environmental governance.

title: Revealing Manager Skill through Path-Dependent Risk Management
affiliations: ,  and BYU Marriott School of Business

detail.title: Revealing Manager Skill through Path-Dependent Risk Management
detail.abstract: Sharpe (1994) demonstrated that distinguishing investment skill from luck requires a substantial number of observation periods. But active managers in delegated relationships are typically evaluated over rolling three-year windows where statistical noise can dominate the signal, leading to the termination of skilled managers due to measurement error rather than a lack of ability. While goal-based portfolio choice and dynamic risk management have been studied, existing research does not provide an explicit solution for optimal tracking error management under delegated mandate structures and rolling evaluation windows. This paper develops a path-dependent risk management framework to address this gap. Using dynamic programming, we solve for optimal tracking error adjustment within client-specified bands as a function of accumulated performance and time remaining. Our primary contribution is demonstrating that relaxing risk bands from ±20% to ±50% around a target active risk (e.g., 4% tracking error), combined with dynamic risk management, substantially reduces statistical noise in performance evaluation. Dynamic policies reduce the probability of negative three-year returns by 11 percentage points (54% relative improvement) and improve ten-year survival of skilled managers from 33% to 56%. The prescribed behavior-reducing risk when ahead and increasing risk when behindmirrors patterns documented in the mutual fund tournament literature (Brown, Harlow, and Starks 1996, Chevalier and Ellison 1997). However, rather than agency-driven gaming, we demonstrate this represents the optimal response to measurement noise in finite evaluation periods. Our framework applies across various tracking error targets and asset classes, with results that are scale-invariant in the relative width of risk bands.

title: Impact of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana -Gramin (PMAY-G) on Income and Employment

detail.title: Impact of Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana -Gramin (PMAY-G) on Income and Employment
detail.abstract: This report  evaluates the macroeconomic impact of the Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana - Gramin (PMAY-G) on income and employment in India up to March 2018 . Using a dual methodology that combines specific rural housing design templates to estimate direct labor requirements and Input-Output (IO) analysis to capture broader inter-sectoral linkages, the study finds that the scheme generated approximately 52.47 crore person-days of direct employment, comprising 20.85 crore skilled and 31.62 crore unskilled person-days . With a total cumulative expenditure of Rs 35,135 crore, the program created an estimated 94.53 lakh additional jobs in the economy, translating to a 1.77% increase in total employment, while simultaneously boosting residential construction production by 22.67% and the overall Gross Value Added (GVA) by 0.55% . Furthermore, scenario analysis based on varying levels of beneficiary financial contribution suggests that total job creation could range between 63.31 lakh and 92.78 lakh jobs, highlighting the scheme's significant multiplier effect on the rural economy

title: Risk Analysis of Bank Guarantee in Trade Finance: A Study on EXIM Bank of India

detail.title: Risk Analysis of Bank Guarantee in Trade Finance: A Study on EXIM Bank of India
detail.abstract: Bank guarantees are a critical instrument in trade finance, enabling exporters to secure contracts and facilitate cross-border transactions without immediate cash outflows. While these instruments support international trade, they also create off-balance-sheet exposures for banks in the form of contingent liabilities, which may crystallize into actual obligations upon invocation. This study examines the risk exposure arising from the issuance of bank guarantees by the Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank of India). Using secondary data from EXIM Bank’s annual reports for the period FY 2021–22 to FY 2024–25, the study analyses trends in non-funded facilities, the growth and share of bank guarantees, and movements in contingent liabilities. The findings indicate a significant expansion in guarantee-based exposure and notable volatility in contingent liabilities, highlighting rising off balance-sheet risk for the Bank. The study underscores the importance of understanding and monitoring guarantee-related exposures, particularly in development-oriented financial institutions supporting international trade.

detail.abstract: This study provides an empirical evaluation of generative artificial intelligence's capacity for investment portfolio construction, specifically comparing AI-generated portfolios with those developed through traditional human methods. Through a controlled experimental framework that employs identical historical data, asset universes, and risk-return metrics, the research examines two prominent large language models, such as GPT and Gemini, under both autonomous and assisted data processing conditions. The findings reveal that while AI demonstrates proficiency in executing straightforward tasks such as equal-weight allocations and provides reasonably accurate directional market judgments over short horizons, it exhibits significant limitations in mathematical precision, constraint adherence, and long-term performance stability. Notably, the study identifies superior out-of-sample performance of simple equal-weight strategies compared to theoretically optimized maximum Sharpe ratio portfolios, challenging conventional portfolio optimization assumptions. The research further establishes that data quality fundamentally determines AI output reliability, with clean inputs enhancing result accuracy and consistency. These insights contribute to the growing literature on AI in finance by offering concrete evidence about its current capabilities and constraints, while providing practical recommendations for investors seeking to responsibly integrate AI tools into their decision-making processes. The study ultimately positions AI as a complementary analytical tool that requires rigorous verification for effective application in portfolio management.

detail.abstract: Fruit and vegetable (F&V) production is insufficient to meet dietary recommendations globally, including in Tanzania. This study assessed agricultural production impacts of a package of sustainable agricultural production interventions. We used data from the first year of an ongoing cluster partially-randomised controlled trial implemented in Tanzania (2023-2030). Thirty-three villages were partially randomised into a control group, which received no interventions (10 villages), or a supply group, which received the agricultural interventions (23 villages) - seed provision, agricultural production, and post-harvest management training. At baseline (Oct 2023-Jan 2024), 2,611 households were enrolled, and 95% were followed-up ~11 months later (Sep-Nov 2024). Linear mixed effects models were used to estimate the change over time and intention-to-treat intervention impacts on vegetable, fruit, and staple crops production. Models applied propensity score weights to account for the partial randomisation. Between baseline and follow-up, the number of months of vegetable production increased by 1.5 months or 88% (incidence rate ratio (IRR) 1.88 (95% CI 1.44, 2.45)) and the number of fruits cultivated by 0.4 fruit or 56% (IRR 1.56 (95% CI 1.13, 2.16)). There were no other changes during this year of implementation in other outcomes examined. After one-year of implementation start, the agricultural interventions had no impact on the number of months of vegetable production; the number of vegetable, fruit, or staple crops produced; the total quantity produced or total yield of each crop type. This lack of impact may be due to the short observation period, limited intervention scale and intensity, or targeting approach.

title: The Macroeconomic Cataclysm: Modeling the Expected Economic Impacts of a Hypothetical Third World War in 2026

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Cataclysm: Modeling the Expected Economic Impacts of a Hypothetical Third World War in 2026
detail.abstract: This paper constructs a structured, forward-looking economic analysis of a hypothetical Third World War initiated in 2026. Employing a qualitative scenario-building methodology, the analysis extrapolates from the economic history of 20th-century total wars and integrates contemporary understandings of global systemic risks, including financial interconnectedness, complex supply chains, and weaponized interdependence. The model delineates the immediate, medium-term, and long-term consequences across critical domains: financial market collapse, supply chain paralysis, stagflation, sovereign debt crises, the devolution of globalization, technological regression, and exacerbated inequality. A dedicated examination of the transition to a "war economy" outlines probable policy responses. The paper concludes that the economic costs would be catastrophic, intergenerational, and fundamentally transformative, providing a powerful, non-ideological economic rationale for prioritizing diplomatic conflict prevention and reinforcing multilateral cooperation as the paramount investment in global economic stability.

detail.abstract: Banning money in markets for goods like education or health is a common policy to prevent unfair access by the wealthy. We investigate whether this policy is well-targeted for its intended goal. For this, we introduce a fairness criterion called discrimination-freeness which requires that goods are allocated independently of wealth. Using a model where willingness to pay increases with income, we find the answer depends critically on the level of wealth inequality. When inequality is high, a transfer ban is a well-aligned policy. It is then no more restrictive than requiring discrimination-freeness. The resulting allocations are constrained-efficient, meaning that any Pareto improvement would be discriminatory. When inequality is low, however, a transfer ban can be overly restrictive, as using monetary transfers may improve outcomes without causing discrimination. Our findings suggest that societies with more equitable wealth distribution may have more flexibility to use price mechanisms than those with high inequality.

title: Unraveling the Effects of Leadership and Motivation Factors on Employee Engagement: Evidence from the U.S. Federal Agencies

detail.title: Unraveling the Effects of Leadership and Motivation Factors on Employee Engagement: Evidence from the U.S. Federal Agencies
detail.abstract: This article discusses employee engagement, a distinct construct in the field of human resource management and development that enhances public sector performance and employee well-being. While many studies have explored a set of determinants of employee engagement, few have examined the relationship between senior executive leadership in the senior executive service (SES) and motivation factors (i.e., intrinsic motivation and empowerment). This article shows that two types of leadership in the SES are strongly associated with employee engagement, and that intrinsic motivation and empowerment are effective mediators of the relationship between SES and employee engagement. Using the Merit Principles Survey 2010 and insights from a set of organizational theories, this study develops an antecedent-mediator-outcome model. It empirically examines the direct and indirect effects of SES and motivation factors on employee engagement. The results showed that political senior executive leadership is positively related to empowerment but negatively related to intrinsic motivation. On the other hand, career senior executive leadership is highly associated with intrinsic motivation and empowerment. The relationship between the SES and employee engagement is partially mediated by the employee’s intrinsic motivation and empowerment.

title: AI Infrastructure Centralization and Technological Autonomy in the Global South

detail.title: AI Infrastructure Centralization and Technological Autonomy in the Global South
detail.abstract: The centralization of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure presents a strategic challenge for companies in the Global South, as it compromises their digital sovereignty, economic competitiveness, and geopolitical security. The concentration of data and computational power in a handful of global technology providers whose headquarters and technological origins are rooted in advanced economies limits local innovation, hinders the development of autonomous technological ecosystems, and exposes these countries to structural dependency on foreign infrastructures. This research aims to understand the implications of such centralization, focusing on how it affects the technological autonomy and strategic positioning of companies in the Global South, examining the structural, economic, and geopolitical dimensions through which this dependency manifests itself and reshapes local technological ecosystems. The methodology is qualitative, based on semi-structured interviews with senior executives responsible for technology and digital strategy in well-established companies founded in the Global South, seeking to investigate how AI infrastructure centralization affects the technological autonomy of companies in emerging economies. As a practical contribution, this research proposes a theoretical framework to support the formulation of business strategies aimed at building more resilient AI ecosystems, contributing to mitigate the exposure of emerging countries to “digital colonization” and strengthen their position in the global digital economy.

detail.abstract:
Ranked-Choice Voting: What is It?

Ranked-choice voting (RCV) has emerged as an increasingly partisan issue in American electoral politics. After initial momentum in 2022 with implementation in Maine and Alaska, RCV experienced significant setbacks in 2024: Ballot measures failed in six states, Nevada reversed its 2022 approval, and seventeen states have enacted legislative bans.

Under RCV, voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate achieves a majority of first-place votes, the last-place finisher is eliminated and the votes of all who ranked that candidate first are transferred to the second-choice candidates. The process repeats until a candidate secures a majority. Proponents contend RCV reduces “spoiler” effects from minor-party candidates and expands voter choice. Critics argue it introduces unnecessary complexity and can produce counterintuitive results.

Who likes RCV?

One might expect partisan preferences for RCV to vary by local context—Republicans favoring it where right-leaning minor parties compete, Democrats where left-leaning parties attract votes.  However, contemporary positioning on RCV does not follow this geographic logic; partisan alignment appears relatively uniform across different electoral contexts. 

For instance, 2024 referendum results demonstrate consistent positive associations between Republican vote share and opposition to RCV. Across eight states and five municipalities, the higher the Trump vote, the lower the RCV support. In Alaska, where voters narrowly rejected repealing RCV by 0.2 percentage points (despite pro-RCV forces having outspent opponents $14.6 million to $500,0), district-level results showed near-linear correlation between Republican presidential support and anti-RCV voting. Nevada’s identical referenda in 2022 and 2024 showed most counties shifting both toward Republicans and against RCV. 

Legislative Division

Legislative voting patterns reveal even more pronounced partisan divisions. Across seventeen states that have banned RCV since 2022, most roll-call votes show Republican legislators voting nearly unanimously to prohibit the system and Democratic legislators voting nearly unanimously against such bans. 

Political discourse has centered on procedural questions, with Republicans citing voter confusion and delayed tabulation and Democrats questioning the necessity of banning an unused system. Academic research provides context for both perspectives: RCV does introduce specific complications—including scenarios where additional support can paradoxically harm a candidate—yet studies examining effects on voter confusion, campaign civility, and turnout have produced mixed results.

Implications 

While RCV has a long history in the United States, the current backlash against RCV appears strongly (though not perfectly) partisan and largely disconnected from this empirical evidence. However, the authors argue that much work remains to fully understand the partisan dimensions of RCV support, requiring deeper analysis of aggregate votes, voter files, ballot-image data, surveys, and campaign rhetoric. Critically, they contend that the increasingly common assumption that RCV primarily benefits Democrats over Republicans remains largely untested, with effects likely more complex and conditional than widely recognized. The authors urge advocates and opponents alike to resist viewing electoral reform through a reflexive partisan lens, instead engaging seriously with logic and evidence. Election rules, they argue, are too consequential to be dismissed as arcane technicalities or resigned to as inherently unfair.

detail.abstract: We use a bi-level framework to address how transmission planning may adapt to the cost of damage from emissions and imperfect competition in both greenfield and brownfield settings. Our upper level comprises a welfare-maximising transmission planner who internalises the damage cost in anticipation of generation operations at the lower level by profit-maximising firms. In a greenfield setting, i.e., without any existing capacity, complete carbon taxation on firms is optimal under perfect competition, and the carbon tax monotonically increases transmission capacity. By contrast, Cournot behaviour by industry chokes off consumption, thereby limiting the damage from carbon emissions and rendering partial carbon tax optimal. In a brownfield Western European setting with perfect competition, only complete internalisation of the cost of damage from emissions provides the price signal to reduce consumption and to spur generation investment as in the greenfield setting. However, the brownfield setting with Cournot behaviour leads to fossil-fuel expansion by price-taking fringe firms, which exacerbates damage from carbon emissions vis-à-vis the greenfield setting. Hence, it is optimal to fully internalise the cost of damage from emissions with complementary expansion of the transmission network in a brownfield setting even with market power in contrast to the result in a greenfield setting.

detail.abstract: This study examines the evolving landscape of anti-tax avoidance measures in the European Union (EU), focusing on the interplay between the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD), the EU Blacklist Code of Conduct on Business Taxation, various unilateral regulations, and the global minimum tax. Drawing on a comprehensive survey of local tax experts, we investigate how Member States have implemented the five core ATAD measures-interest barrier rules, exit taxation, controlled foreign company (CFC) rules, hybrid mismatch provisions, and general anti-abuse rules (GAAR)-as well as the EU Blacklist and additional national provisions such as royalty deduction limitations. The findings reveal a generally consistent adoption of ATAD rules, albeit with notable variation in strictness and scope across Member States. Furthermore, the study evaluates the interplay with the newly introduced global minimum tax. While this global measure primarily targets rate-based profit shifting, our analysis indicates that it may reinforce or partially overlap the EU's other directives-especially for countries that have already implemented extensive anti-tax avoidance legislation. We conclude by highlighting areas where policy refinements could enhance coherence-reducing complexity, avoiding double regulation, and strengthening the overall framework for combating tax avoidance within the EU.

title: Treasury Supply, Relative Convenience Yields and Exchange Rates
affiliations: University of Basel - Center for Economic Science and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: Treasury Supply, Relative Convenience Yields and Exchange Rates
detail.abstract: The fiscal sustainability of US public debt depends crucially on the convenience yield, the premium that investors pay to hold US Treasury. Theoretically, government debt in equilibrium is negatively associated with the convenience yield, which is also linked to the exchange rate through interest parity. However, the existing literature offers only correlational evidence, disregarding the active choice of debt issuance by the government. Using a simple open-economy model with optimal debt supply and liquidity preference for Treasuries, we show that outward shifts in debt supply reduce the convenience yield through dollar depreciation. Conversely, changes in liquidity preference generate positive comovements between debt supply, currency appreciation, and convenience yields. As a result, estimation strategies, like OLS, that fail to disentangle Treasury supply and demand shocks result in an understatement of the yield elasticity of Treasury demand, and of the impact of Treasury supply shocks on exchange rates. We confirm the predicions of our model via local projections using an instrument based on Treasury futures price changes following auction announcements. An unexpected rise in US Treasury supply lowers the convenience yield and depreciates the dollar against G10 currencies by up to three times more than previously esimated.

detail.abstract: Contemporary labor market friction is often attributed to skills gaps or shifting worker preferences. This paper argues that the primary driver of inefficiency is the structural architecture of Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). Originally designed to manage administrative volume, ATS have evolved into filtering mechanisms rather than matching systems-extracting unpaid labor from job seekers, white-labeling decision-making to obscure accountability, and systematically degrading the remaining talent pool (Fuller, Raman, & Sage-Gavin, 2021; Trumble, 2025). Applying Akerlof's "Market for Lemons" (1970) and the framework of Non-Converging Nash Equilibria, this analysis demonstrates how ATS-driven exclusion creates perverse incentives: firms adopting filtering systems to manage application volume collectively undermine labor market efficiency, suppress wages, and distort the allocation of talent (Rochet & Tirole, 2003; Resnick & Zeckhauser, 2002). The dysfunction is inherent to the system itself, not a failure of calibration, and cannot be corrected by operational tweaks alone; meaningful reform requires rethinking the architecture of digital hiring systems to restore transparency, two-sided accountability, and market-clearing mechanisms (Trumble, 2026; Reuters, 2018).

detail.title: The Value of Compliance Offsets in Cap-and-Trade Markets
detail.abstract: We study compliance carbon offsets in cap-and-trade markets. We develop a model predicting that firms sort into offset use by carbon productivity: highly productive firms rely solely on allowances, while less productive firms use offsets because they trade at a discount but carry invalidation risk. Using administrative data from California's cap-and-trade program, we find strong empirical support for these predictions. Structural estimation suggests that roughly one-third of compliance offsets fail to reduce emissions, generating about 2 percent uncounted emissions. Nevertheless, offsets can increase efficiency relative to an equivalent tightening of the emissions cap under certain conditions.

detail.title: From States to Neighborhoods: Measuring Inequality Across Spatial Scales with Satellite Imagery
detail.abstract: Place-based policies and environmental shocks can have heterogeneous distributional effects, yet empirically assessing these consequences is difficult because inequality measures remain spatially coarse. We develop a satellite-based framework to measure neighborhood-level inequality in durable assets and propose a bottom-up aggregation scheme based on the Law of Total Variance to recover inequality for any policy-relevant geography. Using Mexico's 2020 census data on 35 million households, we demonstrate that our approach recovers inequality across spatial scales with substantial accuracy, improving as predictions aggregate from neighborhoods to municipalities. We illustrate the method's utility by constructing the first annual municipal panel of inequality (2017–2024). Using synthetic difference-in-differences, we estimate that a border-region tax-and-wage reform (the Northern Border Free Zone) reduced relative inequality by 0.18 standard deviations, while Hurricane Otis increased it by 0.13 standard deviations. We also find that while pre-existing inequality does not limit the benefits of progressive policy, it significantly amplifies vulnerability to adverse shocks.

detail.abstract: Vegetable prices exhibit large volatility and are generally a major contributor to India's food and headline inflation. This volatility is often exacerbated by supply-side disturbances, predominantly driven by weather shocks, warranting a regular and careful track of evolving weather conditions. This study investigates how weather anomalies, particularly in rainfall and temperature, affect vegetable prices in India. Empirical results suggest that weather anomalies affect vegetable prices, with temperature anomalies having a more immediate impact. Moreover, the impact of temperature anomalies has increased in recent periods, highlighting the need for faster adoption of temperature-resistant crop varieties to support price stability.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we propose a new approach to Asian options pricing under the Black-Scholes model that is based on the observation that, if the asset price follows a geometric Brownian motion, then the Laplace transform of the reciprocal of the arithmetic average of the asset price conditional on the price level at the endpoints of the given time period is known fully explicitly. Based on this, we propose two new option pricing formulas. In the first, we approximate the conditional distribution of the reciprocal of the arithmetic average with a gamma random variable and develop a fast and accurate approximating formula for Asian option prices. In the second, we develop a semi-analytical option pricing formula based on the numerical inversion of the aforementioned conditional Laplace transform, which provides an efficient and extremely accurate solution for the price of a large class of Asian-style derivatives, such as floating-strike Asian options and Australian options. Finally, we show how the proposed pricing approach can be applied to more complex models than Black-Scholes.

detail.abstract: This paper examines recreational anglers' preferences for offshore man-made structures, focusing on standing energy rigs, reefed rigs, and other artificial reefs. We collected geospatial revealed preference data on anglers' fishing trips using an interactive map in a survey of Texas saltwater recreational anglers, which are jointly estimated with stated preference data from a discrete choice experiment. Results from a generalized multinomial logit model show that all three types of structures are significantly valued by anglers. Standing rigs and reefed rigs are valued similarly, and both are valued more highly than other artificial reefs. We also find that anglers exhibit distinct preferences across regions. These findings suggest that rigs-to-reefs conversion could sustain angler visits and mitigate negative social and economic impacts arising from rig decommissioning. We recommend that policymakers prioritize reefing efforts in targeted areas to improve policy decision-making and resource management.

detail.abstract: We present a behavioral definition of an agent's perceived implication that uniquely identifies a subjective state-space representing her view of a decision problem, and which may differ from the modeler's. By examining belief updating within this model, we formalize the recent empirical consensus that reducing uncertainty improves contingent thinking, and propose a novel form of updating corresponding to the agent 'realizing' a flaw in her own thinking. Finally, we clarify the sense in which contingent thinking makes state-bystate dominance more cognitively demanding than obvious dominance.

title: Subsidies versus Tradable Credits for Electric Vehicles: The Role of Market Power in the Credit Market

detail.title: Subsidies versus Tradable Credits for Electric Vehicles: The Role of Market Power in the Credit Market
detail.abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption expands, policymakers consider tradable emission credit systems to replace purchase subsidies. This switch not only eliminates subsidy expenditures but also introduces a credit market with two-sided market power: conventional automakers demanding credits act as an oligopsony, while EV makers supplying credits act as an oligopoly. I develop a theoretical framework in which firms leverage their market power in the output market to manipulate the credit price, which encourages them to raise the prices of their primary fuel-type vehicles. To evaluate the welfare implications, I estimate a structural model that accounts for equilibrium product portfolios, vehicle prices, and the credit price, using data from forty major cities in China. Eliminating subsidies reduces total surplus by about 47 billion RMB per year, while firms' strategic behavior under credit trading further reduces consumer surplus by about 20 billion RMB, with losses exceeding gains in profits and environmental benefits.

detail.title: AI Infrastructure and Financial Markets: Evidence from OpenAI Outages
detail.abstract: This study examines how financial markets respond to disruptions in AI-based information processing. We examine 207 documented OpenAI service outages between April 2021 and August 2025 as quasi-exogenous shocks to market information infrastructure. Across 11,978 affected firms, abnormal trading turnover increases on outage days. Liquidity drops, with Amihud's illiquidity measure implying a 5.8 basis point (bps) higher price impact (per unit of volume) during outages. Abnormal absolute returns are 1.4 bps lower on outage days and abnormal returns are-9.2 bps lower. The impact of outage duration is non-monotonic: returns are most affected by short outages, turnover by intermediate-length outages, and illiquidity by long outages. Overall, our findings suggest that AI systems are now an integral component of modern market infrastructure, with AI outages being associated with significant disruptions in trading activity.

detail.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence in educational settings has prompted institutions to consider restrictive policies that limit student access to AI tools. However, such an approach fundamentally misunderstands both the pedagogical opportunities AI presents and the practical realities of enforcement. Rather than restricting access, educators should redesign assessment practices to emphasize deliverable quality, critical evaluation skills, and the strategic use of AI as a professional tool.

detail.abstract:

detail.abstract: This article examines how affective climate polarization shapes support for climate and just transition policy bundles in western Canada. We draw on an online survey of 3,400 residents in non-metropolitan communities across British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The study combines feeling-thermometer measures of emotional warmth toward climate and political groups with a factorial vignette experiment in which respondents evaluate four climate policies (two carbon taxes and two regulatory mandates), each presented alone and in combination with five just transition supports. Mixed-effects models show that affective climate polarization strongly differentiates overall levels of policy support and, crucially, the flexibility of those attitudes. Respondents who scored high on affective climate polarization held relatively stable views and were either largely unmoved by just transition and climate-policy bundling or, in some cases, reacted negatively. By contrast, individuals with weaker or mixed affective attachments were most responsive. Just transition bundling increased support for both consumer and industrial carbon taxes but had more mixed effects for regulatory mandates. The findings highlight how emotional climate identities structure both the reach and the limits of climate policy design in fossil-fuel regions.

detail.abstract: To study the non-currency risk premia embedded in emerging market (EM) local currency (LC) government bond yields, I examine the Domestic Bond Premium (DBP): the yield spread between government and supranational bonds in the same currency and maturity. Using security-level data from nearly 1,300 AAA-rated supranational bonds across 11 EM currencies, I document that the DBP is frequently negative. Moreover, the DBP remains relatively stable during periods of financial stress when government LC yield spreads over US Treasuries widen dramatically. These patterns cannot be fully explained by default risk and liquidity premia. The empirical evidence instead points to financial repression-policies that generate inelastic domestic demand for government debt-as a potentially important factor in the pricing of EM LC government bonds.

detail.abstract: Standard Distributional Synthetic Controls (DSC) estimate counterfactual distributions by minimizing the Euclidean L2 distance between quantile functions. We demonstrate that this geometric reliance renders estimators fragile: they lack informative gradients under support mismatch and produce structural artifacts when outcomes are multimodal. This paper proposes a robust estimator grounded in Optimal Transport (OT). We construct the synthetic control by minimizing the Wasserstein-1 distance between probability measures, implemented via a Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (WGAN). We establish the formal point identification of synthetic weights under an affine independence condition on the donor pool. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that while standard estimators exhibit catastrophic variance explosions under heavy-tailed contamination and support mismatch, our WGAN-based approach remains consistent and stable. Furthermore, we show that our measure-based method correctly recovers complex bimodal mixtures where traditional quantile averaging fails structurally.

detail.abstract: We develop a menu-cost model with firm-level production networks to study how price adjustments by a small fraction of firms propagate to the macroeconomic level. detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) practices and cloud-native architectures has significantly expanded the attack surface of modern FinTech software systems, increasing exposure to sophisticated and fast-evolving cyber threats (Ananya, David, and Samir 134). While traditional static application security testing (SAST) and dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools remain foundational, they are increasingly limited in their ability to detect complex, context-aware, and zero-day vulnerabilities, often generating high false-positive rates and delayed remediation cycles (Paidy 57). To address these limitations, this study proposes an AI-enhanced hybrid vulnerability discovery framework that integrates static code analysis, dynamic runtime inspection, and continuous learning mechanisms (Bakane, Lindroos, and Mohammad). The framework employs AI-driven static analysis models to identify latent code-level weaknesses, dynamic behavioural monitoring to capture runtime anomalies, and feedback-driven retraining pipelines that enable continuous adaptation to emerging threat patterns (AI-Powered Payment Fraud Signature Generation). Experimental evaluation within FinTech CI/CD environments demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves higher vulnerability detection accuracy, significantly reduces false positives, and accelerates remediation timelines when compared to conventional rule-based security testing methods (Intelligent CI/CD Pipelines Using AI-Based Risk Scoring). The findings indicate that AI-enhanced hybrid vulnerability discovery not only improves technical security outcomes but also strengthens governance, risk, and compliance readiness in FinTech application development, supporting resilient and secure software delivery at scale (System and Method for Secure AI-Based Financial Technology Governance Risk Management).

detail.abstract: The post-Second World War international order is increasingly strained by power diffusion, declining hegemonic capacity, and the normalization of transnational crises that resist resolution. While much scholarship interprets this condition as a return to multipolarity, this paper argues that such diagnoses are incomplete. The defining challenge of the contemporary system is not merely the redistribution of power, but the absence of a viable framework for governing continuous global risk in the absence of a single guarantor-conditions under which systemic harm increasingly emerges through routinized, procedurally justified action rather than overt aggression. The paper advances Multi-Polar Stewardship as an analytic governance framework for a post-hegemonic world. It reconceptualizes international order as a function of distributed responsibility calibrated to capacity, rather than dominant enforcement or ideological convergence. Drawing on international relations theory, global governance scholarship, crisis management, and public administration ethics, the framework specifies the conditions under which stewardship behaviors may emerge among self-interested actors operating under anarchy. It identifies the mechanisms through which capacity-based obligation, performance-based legitimacy, and escalation restraint can stabilize high-risk systems while preserving rivalry below catastrophic thresholds and limiting the normalization of systemic irresponsibility. Through comparative analysis and case applications-including artificial intelligence risk, financial contagion, climate adaptation and migration, and cyber and space escalation-the paper demonstrates how stewardship logic already operates implicitly in domains where traditional models fail. It concludes by outlining implications for policy and research, arguing that in an era of permanent crisis and fragmented authority, system survivability depends less on dominance than on disciplined responsibility and institutional designs that constrain harm without requiring centralized authority.

detail.abstract:
Modern economies operate under unprecedented acceleration—driven by AI, financial automation, shortened decision cycles, and a rising mismatch between systemic speed and human cognitive capacity. Traditional macroeconomic frameworks assume temporal neutrality: that the speed of systems does not materially distort economic behavior. This assumption no longer holds. This paper introduces GHDP™ — the Gross Human Dynamics Product, the first macrofinancial framework modeling time as a priced economic variable. GHDP formalizes how human temporal capacity, system aeration, and institutional integration constraints interact to generate tempo-based economic divergence, shaping productivity, stability, and long-run welfare.

We provide a mathematical definition of GHDP, derive its core components, and demonstrate how temporal disequilibrium creates measurable distortions in labor productivity, consumer decision quality, financial stability, and policy transmission. Finally, we outline implications for central banks and propose a new paradigm: Tempo Governance™

detail.abstract: Previous research has explored host communities' attitudes toward displaced individuals, but much less is known about what displaced people seek in a host community. Understanding both perspectives is key to fostering successful local integration. We address this gap through a randomized conjoint experiment in which nearly 2,000 respondents in the Kasai region of the Democratic Republic of Congo-internally displaced persons (IDPs), returned IDPs, repatriated refugees, and members of the host community-evaluated hypothetical host communities, imagining where they would prefer to settle if forced to flee. Results indicate that, beyond safety, respondents prioritize job opportunities while also valuing social networks and political participation. Preferences are largely similar across groups. The findings suggest that the promotion of economic opportunities and inclusive governance are among the most effective strategies to create conditions conducive to local integration.

detail.title: Moral of Equilibrium: A Systemic Model of Moral Stability in Complex Social Systems
detail.abstract:
Moral of Equilibrium develops a system-philosophical model for analyzing moral stability in complex social systems. Moral is not understood as a normative ideal, a set of rules, or individual intention, but as a structural balance of core variables whose interaction over time determines the sustainability of a system.

The model identifies seven fundamental variables: resources, efficiency, freedom, truth, harmony, justice, and room for action. None of these variables is effective in isolation; stability emerges only through their relational balance. The overemphasis of individual variables does not lead to moral progress but generates structural tensions that destabilize systems over time.

A central feature of the model is its temporal perspective. Moral stability is conceptualized not as a static condition but as a dynamic adjustment process, whose quality is reflected in the magnitude and frequency of corrective interventions required to maintain balance. The model emphasizes judgment over measurement, arguing that quantitative indicators may orient analysis but must not replace responsible decision-making.

Applied to selected case studies from economic and societal contexts, the model functions as a diagnostic framework rather than a prescriptive ethical theory. It offers an analytical language for describing, comparing, and assessing moral structures across different types of social systems.
