detail.abstract: This research explores software engineering, specifically emphasizing the agile programming methodology's crucial role in large-scale development, where effective communication, coordination, and self-management become paramount. As software projects increase in complexity, the study delves into managing inter-team coordination, examining the evolving responsibility principles from small to large projects with multiple agile teams. Beyond assessing inter-team coordination and self-management, the study unveils the influential role of organizational culture in shaping collaborative dynamics within large-scale agile software development. Integrating insights from organizational culture studies, the research aims for a holistic understanding of factors contributing to distributed agile environments, encompassing both technical and cultural dimensions. Recognizing a demand for training underscores the applicability of self-management design as a crucial tool for organizational efficiency. title: Continuous Learning Models for AI-Based Payment Fraud Detection and Signature Evolution
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Continuous Learning Models for AI-Based Payment Fraud Detection and Signature Evolution
detail.abstract: The rapid evolution of payment fraud techniques, driven by sophisticated attackers and emerging digital payment channels, has exposed the limitations of traditional static fraud detection systems. Rule-based and periodically trained models often fail to keep pace with concept drift, leading to declining accuracy and increased false positives as fraud patterns change over time (Maheshkar, Kumar, Sriram). To address this challenge, this study designs and evaluates continuous learning artificial intelligence models capable of dynamically evolving fraud signatures in near real time. The proposed approach integrates incremental data ingestion, adaptive model retraining, and automated feedback loops to ensure sustained learning from newly observed transaction behaviours (Maheshkar, Iseal, and Halli). Empirical evaluation using simulated and real-world payment transaction scenarios demonstrates that continuous retraining significantly improves fraud detection accuracy while simultaneously reducing false positive rates. Moreover, the models exhibit faster adaptation to previously unseen fraud strategies compared to static baselines, highlighting their robustness in highly dynamic threat environments (Singh et al.; Srinivasagopalan). The findings underscore that continuous learning architectures are not merely an optimisation but a structural necessity for modern payment security. This study concludes that deploying continuously adaptive AI systems is essential for building resilient, scalable, and future-proof payment fraud detection frameworks capable of responding effectively to evolving adversarial tactics (Kumar; Sriram).

title: Intelligent FinOps Architectures: AI-Enabled Cost Optimisation and Forecasting in Cloud-Native Financial Platforms

detail.title: Intelligent FinOps Architectures: AI-Enabled Cost Optimisation and Forecasting in Cloud-Native Financial Platforms
detail.abstract: This paper looks at AI-driven FinOps frameworks for cost optimisation and forecasting in cloud-native financial platforms. As more organisations move to cloud-native architectures, managing financial operations well isn't just a nice-to-have anymore; it's critical if you want to stay cost-effective and agile. In this study, we use AI algorithms, predictive models, and cloud-based analytics tools to untangle financial workflows, forecast spending, and right-size resource allocation. Using those methods, we evaluate what happens when AI is added into the mix: does budgeting get better? Do costs come down? Can teams make smarter financial decisions in real time? The short answer is yes. Our key findings show that AI-enabled FinOps significantly improves budgeting accuracy, reveals inefficiencies in cloud resource use, and supports dynamic, data-driven decisions, all of which reduce operational expenses and boost overall financial performance (Sriram et al., 2025; Pasupuleti et al., 2025). We also highlight how predictive analytics and automated insights let organisations manage costs proactively so they can pivot quickly when workloads and cloud usage patterns swing up or down. To be honest, integrating AI into FinOps really changes the game: it moves financial management away from static, spreadsheet-driven practices and toward scalable, adaptive, intelligent cost-optimisation tailored for cloud-native environments. These results underline AI's potential to improve both financial efficiency and strategic agility and offer a practical blueprint for teams looking to get more value from their cloud investments.

detail.abstract: Despite extensive empirical evidence questioning the reliability and predictive validity of informal employment interviews, interviewing remains the dominant selection mechanism in professional services firms. In sectors where human capital constitutes the primary source of value, legitimacy, and competitive advantage, hiring decisions carry strategic, ethical, and reputational consequences. This article advances a conceptual analysis of interviewing in professional services, arguing that prevailing intuition-driven practices function less as neutral assessments of competence than as institutionalised gatekeeping mechanisms that reproduce professional norms, authority, and inequality. Drawing on selection science, strategic human resource management, organisational sociology, and emerging scholarship on AI-enabled hiring, the article examines the limits of intuitive judgment in elite hiring contexts and synthesises evidence supporting structured, evidence-based interviewing approaches. It introduces the Strategic Science Interviewing Model (SSIM), a diagnostic framework comprising four interrelated pillars-scientific rigor, strategic alignment, ethical integrity, and engagement activation-designed to guide the evaluation and reform of interviewing practices in high-stakes professional environments. The article concludes that interviewing should be understood not as an interpersonal art but as a strategic science, particularly as professional services firms increasingly integrate algorithmic and AI-mediated selection technologies.

title: Epistemic Governance: Rethinking Trust in Computational Systems

detail.title: Epistemic Governance: Rethinking Trust in Computational Systems
detail.abstract: As computational systems increasingly shape social, economic, and institutional ecosystems, traditional approaches to governance that are grounded in transparency, control, and predictability are reaching their limits. Many contemporary systems now operate under conditions of uncertainty, adaptivity, and partial observability that challenge the very assumptions on which existing governance models depend. This paper argues that trust under such conditions must be understood as an epistemic rather than purely technical or procedural achievement. It introduces epistemic governance as a conceptual framework for understanding how institutions interpret, contextualize, and act upon system behaviour when certainty cannot be assumed. Rather than offering technical solutions or regulatory prescriptions, the paper reframes governance as an interpretive capacity that enables legitimacy, coordination, and accountability amid complexity. By situating trust within this epistemic context, the paper provides a foundation for understanding how governance can remain meaningful in the presence of autonomous and evolving computational systems, without reducing trust to transparency, control, or compliance.

detail.abstract: Many enterprises struggle with growth stagnation despite sustained effort and continuous innovation. Conventional explanations often attribute such failures to insufficient execution or lack of creativity. This paper argues that a more fundamental cause lies in strategic choices that fail to trigger structural transformation. Building on first-principles reasoning, the study conceptualizes strategy as irreversible choice under uncertainty, introduces the notion of boundary exhaustion, and proposes Ye-Jie innovation as a framework for structural transition. A central contribution of this paper is the introduction of attractors as diagnostic indicators of genuine structural change. When attractors emerge, positive feedback loops become self-reinforcing and growth dynamics increasingly resemble flywheel effects. The paper concludes that sustainable enterprise growth depends not on effort or innovation per se, but on strategic choices that reshape structural conditions.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the structure and performance of modern economies, influencing how resources are allocated, how productivity is enhanced, and how long-term economic growth can be achieved in a sustainable manner. As governments, businesses, and financial systems adopt AI-driven technologies, understanding their broader economic impact has become essential. This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence on sustainable economic growth, with a particular focus on productivity enhancement, innovation dynamics, financial system efficiency, labor market outcomes, and environmental sustainability. The paper adopts a multidisciplinary perspective, integrating insights from economics, technology studies, finance, and public policy. It explores how AI contributes to economic growth by improving decision-making processes, automating routine tasks, reducing information inefficiencies, and enabling data-driven optimization across sectors such as manufacturing, services, finance, energy, and public administration. AI-driven systems enhance productivity by increasing operational efficiency, supporting innovation, and enabling firms to scale more effectively. These gains, when combined with appropriate institutional and policy support, can translate into sustained economic expansion rather than short-term growth spikes. Beyond productivity, the study highlights the role of AI in promoting sustainable economic outcomes. AI applications in energy management, supply-chain optimization, environmental monitoring, and green finance contribute to more efficient resource use and reduced environmental impact. At the same time, the paper recognizes that AI-driven growth is not automatically inclusive or sustainable. Challenges such as labor market displacement, skill polarization, data governance concerns, ethical risks, and unequal access to digital infrastructure may limit the positive impact of AI if left unaddressed. The analysis emphasizes that the overall impact of AI on sustainable economic growth depends heavily on complementary factors, including investments in human capital, digital infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, and institutional capacity. Effective public policies are necessary to ensure that AI adoption supports inclusive growth, enhances resilience, and aligns economic incentives with long-term sustainability goals. The study concludes that artificial intelligence should be viewed as a strategic economic enabler rather than a standalone technological solution. When guided by sound economic policies and governance structures, AI has the potential to support long-term, sustainable economic growth across both advanced and developing economies.

title: When Evidence is Not Enough: How Decision Architecture Sustains Non-Decision in Health Systems

detail.title: When Evidence is Not Enough: How Decision Architecture Sustains Non-Decision in Health Systems
detail.abstract: Health systems repeatedly fail to act decisively in situations where evidence is strong, expertise is abundant, and urgency is widely recognized. These failures are often treated as episodic, attributed to politics, capacity constraints, or leadership shortcomings, despite their recurrence across countries, policy domains, and crisis and non-crisis contexts. This paper argues that such explanations misidentify the binding constraint. Rather than focusing on evidence quality or actor behavior, the analysis examines how decision authority, accountability, and commitment are organized in practice. Using real-world policy episodes diagnostically, the paper identifies recurring failure modes through which health systems generate alignment and activity without closure. These include consensus without commitment, proceduralized delay, defensive reversibility, and misalignment between distributed authority and concentrated blame. Cross-case synthesis reveals a set of reinforcing dynamics that systematically sustain non-decision: diffused authority without integrated ownership, accountability regimes that privilege process over outcome, and asymmetric risk exposure that makes delay safer than commitment. These dynamics persist across routine and crisis settings, differing in tempo rather than structure. The findings suggest that persistent indecision in health systems is not a failure of information or intent, but an outcome of institutional design. Improving performance therefore requires treating decision capacity as a core system capability and redesigning decision arrangements to converge on commitment despite uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Access to organised youth sports in the U.S. has inequities due to intersecting socioeconomic, geographic, and institutional factors. Youth from low-income households, racially and ethnically minoritised communities, and rural or under-resourced urban areas face structural barriers to participation. These include high costs, facility and program quality and low transportation options. These barriers reinforce greater patterns of social inequity (Pérez-Stable and Hooper; Bernhardt et al.). This study constructs a data-driven equity measurement framework to systematically identify and assess inequities in access to youth sports on a cross-community basis. This framework integrates and analyses disparate data streams consisting of population demographics and socioeconomics, spatial distributions of sports facilities, participation and enrollment data, and community-level variables. Using urban analytics and equity-focused integrated data approaches, this framework supports a nuanced, contextual, access condition analysis; a more granular approach to equity measurement (Bibri, Bowers and Choi). Application of the framework shows that inequities in the accessibility of youth sports are not random but are systematically organised by income, race and ethnicity, and urban-rural divides. Communities with the same overall participation rates often have vastly different underlying access conditions, indicating that participation metrics alone have considerable masking disparities. The findings demonstrate the value of integrated, multi-dimensional data approaches in revealing hidden inequities that would have otherwise gone undetected. (Clegg et al.; Kalaba) The main contribution of the study is a scalable and replicable measurement framework that can be utilised by policymakers, planners, and youth sport organisations to monitor and manage inequities, allocate resources, and design strategies that foster a more inclusive youth sport system (Pinkett; Newman et al).

title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How Epistemology Determines Governance Strategy in Authoritarian Regimes
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How Epistemology Determines Governance Strategy in Authoritarian Regimes
detail.abstract:
The comparative analysis of authoritarianism struggles to explain why regimes emerging from similar conditions of systemic stress often adopt diametrically opposed governance strategies. While contemporary structural-demographic models excel at forecasting the temporal onset of crises, they suffer from "morphological blindness" regarding the nature of the successor regime. This paper addresses this predictive gap by proposing the Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis, positing that the operational strategy of a regime is structurally determined by the epistemological architecture of its dominant ideology.

We argue that regimes grounded in Rationalist-Materialist epistemologies (e.g., Marxism-Leninism) are cognitively compelled to adopt an "Engineer" Modality, prioritizing Institutional Capacity (ICI) to minimize entropy. Conversely, regimes grounded in Irrationalist-Mythic epistemologies (e.g., Völkisch nationalism) adopt a "Shaman" Modality, prioritizing Charismatic Mobilization (CMI) to maintain high-voltage ideological intensity.

The framework establishes a universal Two-Phase Model of regime evolution. We demonstrate that all post-crisis regimes begin in a high-CMI "Shamanic" phase driven by the structural necessity of personalized leadership. The critical divergence occurs in the second phase, a process measured by the Cult Trajectory Index (CTI). This derivative metric tracks whether a regime converts charismatic capital into bureaucratic structure or consumes it in radicalization, serving as a leading indicator of long-term survival.

Through a comparative analysis of Stalin’s USSR and Hitler’s Germany, we validate the model, notably reinterpreting Stalin’s Great Purge not as an act of paranoia, but as Structural Resilience Engineering—a rational inter-temporal trade-off that sacrificed military efficiency for political monopoly. Further analysis of the transition from Mao to Deng in China demonstrates the model's ability to track epistemological phase shifts. Ultimately, this paper offers a falsifiable framework for forecasting authoritarian morphology, treating ideology not as rhetoric but as the "cognitive DNA" that programs state behavior.

detail.abstract: The paper presents 'HARM' which is the first holistic Human-centric Ai Risk decision Model. It has been developed using the process of synthesis and tuning based on test results. Built using guidelines from OECD and NIST, the HARM model permits a simple, quick, reliable and holistic calculation of human-centric risk for AI use cases across domains. The clear segregation of risk dimensions, the lookup tables for selection of risk levels and simplicity of risk calculation make HARM easy to understand and adopt. At a time when AI is growing freely because of its complexity, this paper provides a definitive way to manage AI by measuring its risk. Measurement enables the impacts of a technology to be understood and guided. The measurement of holistic AI risk has hitherto not been possible. The HARM model makes it possible. It allows companies to measure the risk of AI use cases during design for safety, governments to specify acceptable risk levels for AI use cases from vendors and standards bodies to build global standards. It presents an opportunity to reduce AI risk levels using a scientific approach. It can bring about a common understanding of AI risk and ways to manage it. HARM is aligned with Responsible AI, Trustworthy AI, Explainable AI and AI for Good. It is hoped that HARM gets adopted across the world to make AI work in human interest.

title: How and when team member exchange and embeddedness mitigate team knowledge hiding: a collaborative team perspective
affiliations: The University of Lahore, Lahore, Pakistan, University of the Punjab, Lahore, Pakistan. and  Aix-Marseille University - CERIC

detail.title: How and when team member exchange and embeddedness mitigate team knowledge hiding: a collaborative team perspective

keywords: Conservation of resource theory Paper type Research paper

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Developing a collaborative view, this study aims to investigate the underexplored role of team social resources, team member exchange (TMX), in mitigating team knowledge hiding (TKH). Specifically, the study examines the underlying psychological mechanisms of team embeddedness (TE) and the boundary conditions of learning orientation (LO) for mitigating TKH, providing fresh insights into team knowledge dynamics. 
Design/methodology/approach: Grounded in the conservation of resources theory, this study tests hypotheses through a quantitative research design. Using a delivery and collection method, three time-lagged surveys gathered multilevel data from 520 employees in 104 teams working in knowledge-intensive IT firms in Pakistan. Multilevel path analysis was conducted using Mplus 8.0. 
Findings: Empirical results revealed that TMX is a deterrent against TKH. Additionally, TE (fit and sacrifice) mediates between TMX and TKH. A multilevel moderated mediation model further shows that members' LO strengthens the effect of TMX on TKH via TE (fit and sacrifice). 
Practical implications:This study provides guidelines for managers and practitioners to mitigate TKH by enhancing socio-psychological resources and fostering individual LO. Originality/value-The existing literature has primarily focused on why, how, and when individuals conceal knowledge in the workplace. However, there is a need to understand how knowledge hiding can be minimized, particularly at the team level. Therefore, this study aims to shift the conversation by addressing a rarely explored research question: How can knowledge hiding in teams be mitigated?

title: 5G and Beyond: Impact on Network Infrastructure and Data Security

detail.title: 5G and Beyond: Impact on Network Infrastructure and Data Security
detail.abstract: The first global implementation of 5G networks and the initial shift towards beyond 5G (B5G) technologies represents a novel era in communication infrastructures that, in addition to ultra-fast global communication and a powerful network flexibility, offers Integrated network management (Ahmad et al.; Samdanis and Taleb). These new technologies continue to address the needs of industry, but also develop new and complex issues of security. This paper offers a critical review of contemporary peer-reviewed literature on the B5G ecosystem and 5G\, industry architectural changes, focusing on changes to threat modeling, security issues, and the range of threat security issues and the range of proposed solutions (Khan et al.; Sullivan et al.). The review concludes that a range of the critical constituent technologies of 5G and B5G (e.g. network function virtualization, software defined networking, network slicing, edge computing, cloud computing, and their convergence, AI based automation on a large scale, Internet of Things (IoT) devices) particularly enhance the size of the network attack surface (Cook et al.; Benzaïd, Taleb, and Farooqi). These characteristics create systemic challenges associated with isolation, trust management, data integrity, and real-time threat detection. Findings suggest perimeter security is ineffective for highly dynamic environments. The study concludes that perimeter security is ineffective for highly dynamic environments. The study concludes that 5G and B5G networks provide significant improvements in performance, scalability, and service agility, the networks require holistic, trust, and AI-based security frameworks that include proactive risk assessment and automated response to create a resilient and secure network infrastructure (Salahdine, Han, and Zhang; Mahyoub et al).

detail.title: Federalism, Procurement Liberalization, and Domestic Review Procedures: The Implementation of the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement in U.S. States and Canadian Provinces
detail.abstract:
The United States and Canada are signatories to the World Trade Organization’s plurilateral Agreement on Government Procurement (GPA). Although they did so at different times, both made commitments that some subcentral entities would be covered, including certain states and provinces. One of the key requirements of the GPA is that its parties must establish review procedures and make them available to suppliers from fellow signatory states. This article considers the extent to which U.S. states and Canadian provinces have implemented that requirement. In brief, it finds that these state and provincial review procedures have many shortcomings, although some of these are perhaps cured by the availability of judicial review. These findings will perhaps be of particular interest to European Union trade negotiators who have long sought greater access to subcentral procurement markets in both markets.

title: Cognitive Defense: Why the Classroom is the New Strategic Battlefield

detail.title: Cognitive Defense: Why the Classroom is the New Strategic Battlefield
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the transition of national security paradigms from territorial defense to "cognitive defense." In the information age, the classroom functions as the "National Sovereignty Reactor," where the collective reasoning (nalar) of a nation is forged. By examining the education systems of the Global South and empirical case studies from Libya, Egypt, Nepal, and Indonesia, this study demonstrates that deficits in critical reasoning create "Peripheral Vulnerability"-a structural weakness exploited by external and internal actors through digital ecosystems, online media, and gaming platforms. The author integrates the "Zero Polar Equilibrium" (ZPE) framework, arguing that global stability can only be achieved through collective moral maturity and cognitive sovereignty. The paper concludes with a 7-Pillar implementation blueprint for urgent educational reform.

title: What You Say Versus When You Say It: Efficiently Predicting Service Completions with LLMs and Stochastic Processes
affiliations: , University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and Technion-Israel Institute of Technology - The William Davidson Faculty of Industrial Engineering & Management

detail.title: What You Say Versus When You Say It: Efficiently Predicting Service Completions with LLMs and Stochastic Processes

declarations.funderStatement: The authors are grateful for the generous support of this work by the National Science Foundation, Division of Civil, Mechanical and Manufacturing Innovation [Award #2441387] (A. Daw) and the United States-Israel Binational Science Foundation [Award #2022095] (A. Daw and G. B. Yom-Tov).

detail.abstract: Accurately determining whether an ongoing service conversation will continue or has effectively ended is central to operational control in chat-based service systems. Premature conversation closures can induce costly customer re-contacts, whereas overly cautious closures waste agent capacity. Using large-scale conversational data from a food delivery service organization, we study two related prediction tasks: short-term conversation continuation and end-of-service completion. We compare three modeling paradigms-stochastic self-exciting point processes, metadata-based neural networks, and large language models (LLMs) operating on full conversation text. Our results reveal a sharp distinction between the tasks. For short-term continuation prediction, lightweight Hawkes process models capture temporal dynamics most effectively and achieve competitive accuracy at minimal computational cost. In contrast, end-of-service prediction benefits substantially from semantic information: a fine-tuned Transformer-based text classifier outperforms all temporal models, while zero-shot prompted LLMs perform poorly despite their scale. A cost-accuracy analysis shows that large models are only justified for specific, high-stakes decisions. Motivated by these findings, we propose a hybrid approach that combines real-time Hawkes-based monitoring with selective LLM queries. This strategy exploits the complementary strengths of temporal and semantic models and achieves a bestof-both-worlds cost-accuracy tradeoff for operational decision-making in service conversations.

title: Export Cartels as a Countermeasure against Trade Friction with the United States: -Japan's Unilateral VER in the Ceramics Industry during the 1950s-1960s

detail.title: Export Cartels as a Countermeasure against Trade Friction with the United States: -Japan's Unilateral VER in the Ceramics Industry during the 1950s-1960s
detail.abstract: As trade liberalization progressed, exporting-country firms tended to mitigate trade friction through coordination with importing-country producers. However, postwar U.S. antitrust laws prohibited such international cartels that undermined competition in the U.S. market. Under these circumstances, Japan's ceramics industry maintained a unilateral VER-a self-restraint regime approaching an export ban-for products deemed likely to directly compete with U.S. goods, although these products held potential to become mainstay ceramic products in the 1950s-60s. This decision was based on market research conducted by government-affiliated organization (JETRO) and the industry itself, as well as the statements and actions of U.S. competitors. The export cartel directed at the U.S. partially resembled a market-sharing international cartel and served to prevent or slow the rise in import restriction risks. Thereby, it illustrates the trade-off between suppressing protectionism and promoting competition within the flow of trade liberalization under the GATT system.

detail.abstract: Global Capability Centres have emerged as important hubs enabling multinational corporations to drive technology-led business innovation and digital transformation. However, even with strong financial backing and sponsorship, a majority of the GCCs underperform across key dimensions of effectiveness such as innovation, market performance and enterprise efficiency. As GCCs strive to move beyond execution excellence to true business impact, the key differentiators of success lie not just in what employees do as part of their formal roles but equally in how they choose to engage with the organisation beyond those roles. Organisational citizenship behaviours (OCBs) – the discretionary individual behaviours that are not explicitly required by formal job descriptions and are not directly recognised by the organisation’s formal reward systems – hold the key to enhanced contextual performance. We break down the seven key dimensions of OCBs – helping behaviours, sportsmanship, organisational loyalty, organisational compliance, individual initiative, civic virtue, and self-development – and link them to success factors for GCC success. Antecedents of OCBs are also briefly explored. The working paper lays some of the groundwork for a planned in-depth literature survey and empirical study involving multiple GCCs.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or clinical trials. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Virtual asset markets exhibit significant heterogeneity in execution quality across exchanges, even for identical trading pairs. Traders frequently observe that price movements depicted on charts do not translate into actual trade executions, leading to failures of conditional orders such as stop-losses. This paper argues that this phenomenon is not a result of trader error but stems from structural differences in market microstructure and liquidity architecture. We introduce a formal framework that decouples price movements from trade executions and propose novel metrics to quantify phantom price movements, order book fragility, and execution continuity. Using high-frequency order book and trade data, we conduct a comparative analysis of fragmented, retail-centric exchanges and institutional liquidity-based execution environments. Our findings reveal that price movements without execution are pervasive in fragmented markets, whereas institutional liquidity environments preserve execution continuity and the validity of conditional orders, even during periods of extreme volatility. These findings have critical implications for risk management, strategy design, and market integrity in virtual asset trading.

title: The Alarming Rise of Cybercrime in India

detail.title: The Alarming Rise of Cybercrime in India
detail.abstract: Cybercrime in India is on the rise in both incidence and complexity, creating a serious threat to individuals, organizations, and the integrity of the nation's digital ecosystem. As measured by the National Crimes Records Bureau (NCRB), the volume of cybercrime in India jumped by over 27% from 2019-2020 and, in total, has surpassed more than 50,000 reported cases in 2021. By 2025, a significant spike in cyber incidents was observed, with 22.68 lakh (2.26 million) occurrences cited in 2024. However, experts as well as government representatives consistently identify that these numbers grossly undercount the prevalence of cybercrime due to the phenomenon of reporting under-counts, or systemic failings in capturing occurrences of cybercrime.

title: Siloed Oversight Why Clean Audits Don't Mean Clean Hands in International Humanitarian Aid
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Siloed Oversight Why Clean Audits Don't Mean Clean Hands in International Humanitarian Aid
detail.abstract:
Federal oversight of international humanitarian aid relies on fragmented disclosure and compliance systems that fail to detect when grantees operate supply chains with alleged terror-linked partners while participating in international boycotts prohibited under U.S. law. This paper documents how organizations can simultaneously file IRS Form 5713 admitting boycott participation, receive unqualified Single Audit opinions, certify anti-terrorism compliance to federal grantors, and maintain "low-risk auditee" status—with no mechanism to surface contradictions to decision-makers.

Using publicly available IRS filings, Federal Audit Clearinghouse records, and USAspending.gov data, the paper presents a case study of two major humanitarian organizations—Americares Foundation ($1.9 billion annual revenue, $16 million federal awards) and American Near East Refugee Aid ($182 million annual revenue, $109 million federal awards)—revealing a bilateral funding relationship where one organization admitted boycott participation the same year it received a clean audit, while the other received a compliance finding for failing to report subaward relationships under the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.

The analysis identifies five systemic failures: (1) siloed disclosure systems where IRS filings are not cross-referenced with grant certifications; (2) Single Audit procedures testing process documentation rather than substantive partner vetting; (3) a "designation gap" where allied foreign intelligence on terror-linked entities is not integrated into U.S. grant decisions; (4) unenforced Schedule F requirements allowing $387 million in foreign grants with zero recipient names disclosed; and (5) a low-risk auditee feedback loop reducing oversight of organizations that evade early detection. Policy recommendations include mandatory cross-referencing of Form 5713 disclosures, substantive partner vetting audits, allied intelligence integration, and enhanced Schedule F enforcement.

title: Epistemic Respect and Intellectual Humility: Foundations for Transformative Organizational Research
affiliations: Quinnipiac University and Oklahoma City University

detail.title: Epistemic Respect and Intellectual Humility: Foundations for Transformative Organizational Research
detail.abstract: In an era marked by unprecedented technological transformation, evolving work arrangements and heightened awareness of equity and inclusion in organizational contexts, the Organization Management Journal finds itself at a critical juncture. The articles featured in this issue, including an examination of affect and attitudes in the gig economy, inclusion strategies for autistic adults in the workplace, and innovative pedagogical approaches to teaching motivation theories, collectively point toward a fundamental need for what we term epistemic respect and intellectual humility in organizational research and management practice. The convergence of these diverse yet interconnected themes presents an opportunity for us to reflect on how we, as scholars and practitioners, approach knowledge creation, validation and application in organizational settings. This editorial argues that epistemic respect and intellectual humility are not merely ethical considerations but foundational principles that can enhance the validity, relevance and transformative potential of our research endeavors.
